speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In my speech, I will deal with the need to set out the laws in written form.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will then take Members through the clauses in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And in doing so, I will deal with concerns that have been raised and some of the points that have been made, as reflected in the Motion of Amendment which has been filed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He said this because the law on contempt developed through the common law over several hundred years and covering different facets.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Thus, to many, including lawyers, it is often a mystery.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Former Chief Justice Chan Sek Keong made this point.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He pointed out that the law on contempt in Singapore was an anomaly and he said all our criminal laws are based on statutes, whereas the law on contempt was not.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Chief Justice (CJ) requested that I consider putting it in statutory form and I agreed with him that I would do so.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In many Commonwealth countries, such as the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand, the law started as a common law offence, and the need for setting it out in writing has been recognised.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Clause 2 of the Bill sets out the interpretation of the key terms used in the Bill, for example, the Courts to which the Bill applies; and when a Court proceeding is "pending".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are other ancillary types of contempt which are also dealt with in this Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Court often directs a person to do something or not to do something.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, take a case where a former spouse applies for maintenance for herself and her children.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In cases where the Court orders maintenance, and if the husband refuses to comply and deliberately chooses not to pay, his former wife and the children suffer.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They may depend on the maintenance to pay for their schooling needs or even their basic necessities.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We undertook significant reforms to the family justice system.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Amongst other things, we improved the enforcement of maintenance orders.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But there are ex-spouses who simply refuse to obey maintenance orders, despite their ability to pay.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are also those cases where, for example, the wife disobeys an order granting the husband access to the children.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For such people, the threat of a significant jail term can help.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They may become more likely to obey Court orders.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Under this law, the defaulter can be punished if he intentionally chooses to disobey the Court's order.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: On the other hand, there is a need to be fair to the person if he honestly and reasonably did not understand what the Court had ordered and the Court takes the view that he ought reasonably to be excused.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Clause 21 of the Bill provides a defence in such a case.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The provision is intended for those who intentionally disobey Court orders.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Court will have to take into account the seriousness of the breach and whether the breach is intentional, in deciding whether to proceed and how to proceed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have given an example of an order from the Family Court which is disobeyed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The rule, of course, applies to other types of Court orders as well.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: To sum up, defaulting parties will face serious consequences if they intentionally disobey the Court's orders.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Such disobedience often takes place in the lower Courts, including the Family Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The intent is to allow the lower Courts to deal with the more serious contemptuous conduct that can occur before those Courts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This will complement other changes we are making to the civil and family justice systems.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the intent is to protect the more vulnerable parties.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They can then receive the full protection of the law.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Clause 3(1)(c) deals with the situation where there is interference with Court proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This can occur where someone disrupts Court proceedings, interferes with witnesses or intimidates them.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Likewise, when someone interferes with, or intimidates judges, parties, lawyers and witnesses.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They should be free from all of these extraneous interferences.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The offence is made out where a person intentionally insults or causes any interruption or intervention to any judge who is sitting in any stage of a Court proceeding, for example, where a person shows up in Court, starts shouting from the public gallery of the Court room, and interrupting ongoing Court proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Court is a place where serious issues are dealt with, some affecting life and liberty, and there is no place for disruptive or insulting behaviour.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Similarly, clause 3(1)(e) also deals with the situation where any other act would interfere, obstruct or cause a real risk of interfering or obstructing, with the administration of justice.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The overarching purpose is to ensure Court proceedings are respected and allowed to complete their full course, without facing obstruction or interference from persons.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will now turn to discuss sub judice contempt, set out in clause 3(1)(b) of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In essence, sub judice contempt deals with conduct, for example publishing something, that would prejudge an issue in pending Court proceedings; and such prejudgment either prejudices or interferes with ongoing Court proceedings, or poses the real risk of doing so.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Others are dealt with by the High Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are thousands of civil cases in the lower Courts and in the High Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Every party to a criminal or civil trial is entitled to a fair trial and everyone facing a criminal charge is entitled to the benefit or the presumption of innocence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These are fundamental pillars of our justice system.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Persons in Court cases should not face prejudgment by the media or the public in a way which whips up sentiment and creates a real risk of interfering with their trials.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Lawyers do as well while their client's case is ongoing.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The test is whether it prejudices or interferes with ongoing Court proceedings or poses a real risk of doing so.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, you have to show that it prejudices or interferes or poses a real risk.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: On these questions, one may have to consider a whole host of factors, including who made the comment, the content of the comment, the extent of the publication, the likely impact on the trial.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the suggestions and the requests are, therefore, requests to change the law as it now stands.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Consider what, in effect, is being proposed with such a suggestion.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we agree to it, we are then saying it is acceptable for the trial to be prejudiced, so long as it is not seriously prejudiced.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A person who is a defendant in a criminal trial could face years in prison.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Do we really want to say that it is acceptable to prejudice his right to a fair trial?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What happens to the presumption of innocence and the basic right to a fair trial?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You balance that against someone's wish to comment on the proceedings, which prejudices the proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You balance the chap in Court who is facing a criminal charge, you balance his rights against somebody else's desire to comment on those proceedings; not just comment, but comment in a way that prejudices those proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is the right that we have to balance against the right of free trial and presumption of innocence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Is it acceptable for such a commentator to say, "Yes, I prejudiced the trial, but I didn't seriously prejudice the trial"?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Why should someone's right to comment, sitting in the security of his home, be given precedence over the right to a fair trial and prejudice a person who faces a jail sentence?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Is it not better to wait for the trial to be over, for the facts to be established, before comments are allowed?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Again, I emphasise, it is not all comments.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are those which prejudice a fair trial or pose a real risk of doing so.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Comments which do not fall into that category are not within the clause.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After the judgment, one can comment as he or she wishes on the judgment on the conduct of the parties.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The words of a New Zealand Chief Justice put it well: "If Joe Public is accused of an offence of which he believes he is innocent, he will not wish to be tried in the media.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When charges are laid in court, the public must be assured the issues will be decided in the court and nowhere else." As Members of the House, ask yourself, each one of you, to bring it to the personal level.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Say someone you know is facing a criminal trial.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Do you want the world saying he is guilty before his guilt or innocence is established?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Do you want his right to a fair trial to be prejudiced and then someone to come and say, "Yes, I prejudiced it, but I did not seriously prejudice it." Do you think that makes good policy?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Another comment that is made against this provision is it "curtails free speech".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You know, to raise this spectre is, by itself, not an argument.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One has to go beyond the rhetoric, get to the specifics.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What is the right that is being curtailed?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What you cannot do is to say something that actually prejudices a specific case.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Again, what you are saying is that an observer's right to speak as he wishes should override a person's right to a fair trial; it does not matter if the trial itself is prejudiced as a result.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You know, most of the people who get charged in the State Courts, they are ordinary folks.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are not lawyers, Members of Parliament or journalists – not usually anyway.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They find themselves on the wrong side of the law.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Do we really want to say, in this House, to the ordinary man in the street that it is okay for his trial to be prejudiced and it is okay for him to be unfairly treated because it is incidental to someone else's right to comment?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Hon Members, the people who are the loudest on these issues are usually the people who can take care of themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I say it is shocking for us to say to such a defendant, "It is okay, my friend, your trial has only been a little bit prejudiced.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So what if the chances of you being found guilty have increased?" If we are not strict, it can easily get out of control and the Courts will lose control, as has happened in other places.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Let us say there is a high profile child rape case.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The child is dead, there is obviously a lot of unhappiness among the general public, and it is high profile, and there is a lot of interest.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Let us say the defendant comes from a certain background, it can be race, it can be religion, it can be education level, sexual preferences – it does not matter, he comes from some background.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Assume the national media were to publish prominent articles on a daily basis saying that people of that particular background, race, religion, educational level or sexual preference are prone to committing these types of offences; and such people should be severely dealt with.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Can such a campaign colour the public mood?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We do not have juries, true, but we have witnesses and we have expert witnesses as well; people who go to court to give evidence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Do we want them to be put under pressure?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Say an expert takes the view on the mental state of the defendant which will potentially give the defendant a defence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Do you want the mass media to carry articles which suggest that such defences are phoney and should not be allowed, that such defendants should be severely punished?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Do we want to get into arguments discussing the media's right to discuss matters of public interest versus the individual's right to a fair trial?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Because the media will say and has said in other countries that the defence, through psychologists and psychiatrists, is a matter of public interest.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And, of course, they are matters of public interest.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But there is a time and place to discuss it.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Can we discuss it after the trial is over?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is not as if these discussions are prevented entirely.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Any expert who wants to give evidence on behalf of the accused runs the risk of being tainted in the opinion of the public.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He does it first time, and, say, he gets a lot of flak.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Do you think he will want to do it a second time or a third time?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The prosecution will also be placed under enormous pressure to charge and secure a conviction.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I had earlier talked about expert witnesses, so in the conduct of the trial, think of other witnesses.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Would they become reluctant to testify because their evidence is contrary to public opinion?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Or would they modify their perception of the evidence?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the public, having already formed an opinion of guilt, would they be able to accept the Court's decision to acquit?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Would they even bother reading the Court's judgment or just assume the Court must have been wrong?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Whatever the outcome, the credibility of the trial and the Court would be damaged.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the Court orders a severe sentence, the public will assume this was because of the media campaign.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the Court acquits the defendant and says the defence succeeded, the public will assume the opposite – that the judge wanted to show that he had not been influenced by the media.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At least some members of the public could assume that.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In either case, the public will question the integrity of the outcome.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These are comments which can prejudice the trial.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Other comments you can make at any time.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Wait for the facts to be established; do not create your own facts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Those have to be established by the Court, whether it is a Coroner's inquiry or a trial.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Then, you can comment on the defendant, the case, the judgment, the general practice, the general policies, on any matter really, subject to other laws.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That way, you know you have a good system, a system that will deliver justice and give everyone a fair trial.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are many examples from other countries where trial by media takes place.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some of you would find the name "Amanda Knox" familiar.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: She, together with two others, was accused of killing her flatmate.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The international media went to town with the story.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Barely a month after the incident, one newspaper published that the victim "it seems, died for no other reason than that she had the terrible misfortune to find herself sharing an apartment with ‘Foxy Knoxy'".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is the moniker they gave her – "Foxy Knoxy".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This conclusion was based on comments that were passed by some unidentified persons.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some newspapers labelled her as a "killer" or "psycho-killer" before the courts had fully determined the matter.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Reading these articles, the natural inclination would be for a member of the public to agree with the tone of the articles, to conclude that the suspect was guilty even before the investigations had been completed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Often, they are based on assertions and evidence that would not stand the scrutiny of a court process.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And, in fact, Ms Knox was eventually acquitted.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We do not want to get into arguments with commentators as to whether what they said may have prejudiced the trial, but it was necessary in public interest; nor do we want to get into an argument where they say, "Well, you know, prejudicing the trial was incidental to my right to speak".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Those with more resources or better access to the media can also abuse such a system.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They will take advantage if we are not strict.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, by starting media campaigns to pressure an accused to plead guilty, or a victim to settle out of Court, justice can become a function of how closely connected one is to media sources or how wealthy one is.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And what happens after the media prints an article that unfairly assumes you are guilty, when you are, in fact, innocent?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The public would not be able to tell which facts are true, which facts are false or irrelevant.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: How then will you clear your name in public?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Will the public believe what you say after a series of articles of such a nature?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It can affect you, your safety, your family's safety, your career, your standing in society.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: All these before the Court has decided on your guilt or innocence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And if the defendant complains, it will be argued that the matters were discussed in the public interest and the prejudice was only incidental.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In effect, the question, therefore, when considering these other suggestions, is whether you want to undermine the presumption of innocence and whether it is fair to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The public and media are also free to debate the merits or demerits of our legislation, even if there are ongoing cases involving such legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Current law and the law as set out in the Bill are the same, and one is not prevented from advocating one's position, for example, on the death penalty even if a capital trial is going on.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Academics or media outlets publish commentaries on a judge's decision, even where an appeal is pending.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Commenting on a judge's reasoning is unlikely to pose a real risk of prejudicing the appeal outcome.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the Bill gets passed, they will continue to be allowed under the Act.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In coming up with this approach, we have, of course, considered the approach in other jurisdictions.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It did so, at least partly, to bring its law in line with European law.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The UK Act came about after the European Court of Human Rights decided, in one case, that the decision of the UK courts did not satisfy the test under the European Convention of Human Rights (ECHR).

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: However, the Australian and New Zealand courts have taken a different position from that of the UK.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Each country will decide for itself what is best in its own interests.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our Courts have set out what the test is for us.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have to chart our course and decide what is in our best interests.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This happens today on a regular basis even before the law.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Take the example where there is a spread of infectious diseases, maybe something like the severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), and say it could potentially be due to negligence, maybe even fraud, on the part of some hospital staff.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And let us say the Police are investigating and proceedings are likely and, say, a Coroner's inquiry has been announced.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Nevertheless, the Government must be able to come out and to set out the facts, as it knows them.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The public needs to know what is happening, what is the likely infection spread, crucially, what are the risks to individuals and what happened at the hospital, as best known at that point in time by the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Say, a bank suffers a run due to a massive fraud by an employee.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The bank may have commenced action immediately and may have obtained injunctions.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They can have serious consequences for the economy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Government must come out and state the facts and the position and, hopefully, reassure the public.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It cannot wait for ongoing Court proceedings to end before informing the public about some matters.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As I said, if we look back, it is not unusual for the Government to come out and make these statements.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is not targeted at any particular individual.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is not targeted at the case per se.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is about what happened so that the public can go about their affairs in a more informed way where there is a specific public interest to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Government statements are usually crafted sensitively to try and avoid prejudicing proceedings, while informing the public, because their own lives, well-being also need to be protected.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And so far, for all the statements that the Government has issued, there has been no suggestion that these actions have prejudiced any proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Bill seeks to set out what is happening and what has happened for many years.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In one or two cases, it was alleged that the statement should not have been made and the Courts have clarified the position.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, in Re Application of Lau Swee Song   SGHC 16, the Court considered the Government's responsibility to come out and deal with matters publicly.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Government will only be allowed to give a factual account and state its position, and that statement will not preclude the Court from exercising its judicial power in relation to the issues at hand.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Courts are integral to a well-functioning democracy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: People must have faith and confidence in them.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: People must have faith and confidence in the administration of justice.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Baseless attacks on the Judiciary erode trust and affect confidence in the administration of justice.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In 2011, he said this: "The rationale of punishing such kind of contempt is to uphold the authority of the Court which is an indispensable institution for the administration of justice...

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We do not mind criticism, even harsh criticism, of the merits or justice of our decisions, on grounds that are not related to our fitness to hold judicial office...

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Those who do not hold judicial office may not fully appreciate or share the same sense of responsibility that a judge holds with regard to his office.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Scurrilous remarks, unless firmly dealt with, would inevitably undermine public confidence in the Judiciary." The High Court of Australia has observed that: "The authority of the law rests on public confidence, and it is important for the stability of society that the confidence of the public should not be shaken by baseless attacks on the integrity or impartiality of courts or judges." The New Zealand courts have said: "Extravagant and inflammatory language, calculated not only to incite disapproval of particular decisions, but also to shake confidence in the courts themselves, and provoke discontent and ill-feeling, is considered so plainly contrary to the public interest as to constitute an offence calling, in proper cases, for the application of the summary power for punishing for contempt...

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Criticism may be strong and forceful, but it is not to be couched in the language of abuse and invective ".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have quoted from other jurisdictions to explain the rationale for the rule.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The precise application of the law, of course, varies from country to country.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you allow constant attacks – attacks, say, of bias and corruption – over time, the public perception of the judiciary will be affected.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will explain later with reference to one country.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I asked for some research in related fields.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Assume there are blatant and unsubstantiated falsehoods about the judiciary repeated often enough, it will affect public confidence in the judiciary.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: An empirical analysis was conducted of British press coverage of the 2009 Ian Tomlinson scandal.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This involved a newspaper vendor who died in the midst of police handling protesters at London's G20 summit.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He died after being pushed by a police officer.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Based on the empirical analysis, commentators concluded that "the emergence of the press politics of outrage is undermining trust not just in the political class as individuals, now a well-rehearsed debate, but in entire institutions".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That means it is undermining confidence and trust in the entire institutions, beyond the politicians.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Politicians are already assumed to be "gone cases", if I can use a colloquial term.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Likewise, in Singapore, if you allow baseless attacks on the Judiciary, you get erosion of trust in the Judiciary.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This does not mean no criticism of the Judiciary is allowed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I read out the extracts from the different judges, including former Chief Justice Chan Sek Keong.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, that is not understood much by people, they think that it precludes any kind of criticism.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It does not mean protecting judges from being criticised in their personal conduct, for example, outside of their conduct as judges.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If they behave badly, they can be criticised.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It does not mean you cannot criticise their judgments.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It does not mean that you cannot criticise the way they conducted trials, as long as no improper motives are ascribed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When people lose confidence in the Judiciary, your entire administration of justice gets affected.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Weigh that against what is it that you are seeking to proscribe?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You are proscribing specific attacks of bias, corruption, favouritism, scurrilous abuse and other allegations of such nature.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Nothing prevents you from attacking the reasoning of the judge, attacking policies reflected in the judgments.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And you are entitled to the full latitude of fair criticism.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And there is a further condition, before the offence is made out.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What you say must pose a risk of erosion of public confidence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Under common law in Singapore, the test is "real risk".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will discuss the reasons for our approach in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Judiciary and the administration of justice are hugely precious assets for us.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We inherited them from the UK and have made them better.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The common law as it is applied in Singapore does not allow our Courts to be debased or scandalised.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Singaporeans, as well as international institutions, hold our Courts in very high regard.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Separately, the State Courts conducted a survey on Court users last year.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is an enviable position to be in.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Judiciary is truly an institution that is held in the highest esteem by Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is the very foundation of the rule of law.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The greater the prestige of the Courts, the greater the authority, and the greater the respect from everyone for that authority.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As was stated by an Australian Court in 1994:"…it is important to remember that … the justification for proceedings for contempt of court… lies not in the protection of the reputation of the individual judge… but in the need to ensure that… courts are able effectively to discharge the functions, duties and powers entrusted to them by the people".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As another court, this time in Ireland in 1991, put it: "  is not committed by mere criticism of judges as judges, or by the expression of disagreement – even emphatic disagreement – with what has been decided by the courts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The right of citizens to express freely, subject to public order, convictions and opinions is wide enough to comprehend such criticism or expressed disagreement.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Such contempt occurs where wild and baseless allegations of corruption or malpractice are made against a court so as to hold the judges to the odium of the people as actors playing a sinister part in a caricature of justice." Again, I refer to these cases: mainly for the expression of the principle on why we have this rule – scandalising the Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Singaporean cases are the ones that matter and the underlying philosophy of the Singaporean cases is similar.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When you have a situation where the Courts are respected, then the administration of justice proceeds smoothly.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And people, whether or not they are satisfied with a judgment, nevertheless, trust the system.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Internationally, what is the standing of our Courts?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: According to the Political and Economic Risk Consultancy (PERC), we are second in Asia for the quality of our judicial and legal system.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The point is this: on one side, the Courts administer justice.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Respect for them, respect for their authority, are a key pillar of society, a fundamental public good for the well-functioning of society.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: On the other hand, weighing against that, what is being curbed?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The right of an individual to abuse the Judiciary, to say judges are biased and corrupt, to scandalise the Courts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: People have the right, as I said more than once, to criticise judgments, to criticise policies, to disagree with rulings and to discuss all of them.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And remember that those who attack the judges fall within a wide spectrum – from the idealistic, to those who are constitutionally sour, to those who are outright dishonest.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some will keep repeating falsehoods or manufacturing facts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some will exploit the position by making personal attacks, sensationalising based on falsehoods for pecuniary profit.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: On one side, you have the sanctity of the Judiciary and the confidence reposed in the Judiciary.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: On the other side, we have some people's desire to launch personal attacks against judges.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is the weighing that one has to do.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In a case in Hong Kong, a newspaper accused the local judiciary of being biased against them.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Among other things, it described the judges as "swinish white-skinned judges", "pigs" and "judicial scumbags and evil remnants of the British Hong Kong government".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ask yourself, what is the benefit of publishing this sort of thing, apart from some perverse form of personal satisfaction from the writer's perspective?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is that which is prohibited in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Bill makes clear that fair criticism is not prohibited and "fair criticism" is defined in case law.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Academics have for many years written articles to criticise judgments.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As I have earlier explained, fair and accurate reporting that is made in good faith will also not be caught.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I should say, by the way, this is also not about protecting the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It has nothing to do with the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Judges should be held to high standards of accountability, like other public servants.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That can include the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau (CPIB).

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If one calls a judge a biased swine, then let us not have arguments as to whether he only risked undermining the sanctity of the Judiciary, as opposed to whether he really risked undermining the sanctity of the Judiciary.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have laid out for Members the different factors, and this is a policy call if we want to go this way.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is for us to decide which is the right approach.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Judges, not in their personal capacity, but judges performing functions.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is a policy call as to why we should give them protection.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This will give us a strong anchoring in the rule of law which, in itself, is of basic fundamental importance for our people.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, quite importantly – the first is the fundamental reason, that alone is enough, but going beyond it – it allows Singapore to be the pre-eminent, vibrant legal centre in the region.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Look at the number of large law firms in Singapore ‒ substantial, given the size of our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Larger economies do not have as many large law firms.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Look at the quality of the profession in Singapore and the international work it gets.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Look at the number of foreign lawyers who are here.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Look at the work that gets done out of Singapore, benefiting us and our economy, which has got no connection to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We stand out in Asia as the jurisdiction of unchallenged independence, impartiality, great judiciary, good lawyers.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is what I am seeking to protect.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Look at the Singapore International Commercial Court (SICC).

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We invited some of the eminent judges from around the world to sit on it and they agreed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Because they have a reputation, and we will protect them, too.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They accept and hear international cases which have little or no connection to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I do not think any other country in Asia could have set up an SICC.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They could have set it up, but it would not succeed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are tremendous benefits from the confidence that comes from us being a vibrant, strong, first-rate legal centre with the Judiciary as its central core.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we did not have a reputation for the rule of law, that would not have happened.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Again, if you allow baseless attacks on a regular basis, you will not have the same perception.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The judges developed the common law based on a strict legal precedent perspective.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we, the Ministry, have a larger policy perspective in terms of the other bits and pieces and aspects of the whole legal spectrum.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And, on that basis, we said, on this one area, let us make it even stricter.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Look at the impact on the economy ‒ travel, tourism, hospitality.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we succeed in making Singapore a legal hub, it will have a tremendous positive impact on the economy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we have a real chance to do that, provided we get it right.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And weigh that, again – I keep coming back to this point – what is it that is being curbed?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Most of us would not want to get out of bed and say something about a judge being a "swine".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is that which is being curbed ‒ allegations that a judge is biased.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You weigh the public good against what is being proscribed and, in my view, the balance is quite clear.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are countries where a view has been taken, that more latitude should be given to attack judges.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is a question for each society, each country to decide, as these other countries have themselves acknowledged.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the words of the New Zealand court, "The complex process of balancing the values underlying free expression and fair trial rights may vary from country to country, even though there is a common and genuine commitment to international human rights norms.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the British High Commission was really serious and sincere, one would have expected them to touch base and talk to us.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, what is the purpose of issuing a public statement the weekend before the Parliament debate?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The purpose seems to be to try and influence the debate, which is quite improper.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It was issued on Friday, on the eve of this debate.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It says it urges Singapore and all countries to abolish the "scandalising the judiciary" offence, and he said it was not specific to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: With the deepest respect to the High Commissioner, one can only say this answer is extremely intriguing.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you want to intervene in a debate and make a comment, then at least have the courage of your convictions and not beat a hasty retreat at the first question.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are a few points I would like to make about the comment from the British High Commission.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, which countries did the British High Commission make this comment to?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Did the British High Commission see fit to make such comments to the Australians?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Or is it that only some ex-colonies are privileged to get such advice from the British High Commission?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If so, I wonder what is the distinction, that we are so privileged?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I should make clear that the laws in respect of scandalising and the defences available vary from country to country, even between Australia, New Zealand, Ireland and us.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have consciously chosen to stick to the law as developed by the Singapore Courts, except for the one change I have mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I am not sure the British High Commission is aware of the circumstances in which the offence of scandalising the court had been abolished in the UK in 2013.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Law Commission noted that "There   a great deal of extremely abusive online material concerning judges".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Law Commission also acknowledged that the UK judiciary had lost the deferential respect it used to enjoy and noted that "this change is one to be regretted".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They were of the view that such a situation could no longer be reversed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The offence had limited symbolic value as everyone was scandalising the court anyway.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It was happening frequently and was rarely prosecuted.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Law Commission also considered that the offence was, in principle, an infringement of freedom of expression, which was a basic right under the European Convention on Human Rights.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: While the Law Commission did not believe that the existence of the offence was contrary to the European Convention, they felt that there was a risk that particular prosecutions may be disapproved by reason of ECHR.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, they recommended that the offence be abolished because the standing of the courts was already damaged in public opinion, a point, which as I said earlier, they noted with "regret".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And keeping the law in the books under such circumstances served no purpose.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Britain, of course, has had an interesting history, as with its membership in the EU.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But I am not sure Britain's experience of changing the law to conform with European human rights laws is completely relevant to us.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the statistics and surrounding facts suggest that what the Law Commission said about the standing of the UK courts is, in fact, true.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Lord Chief Justice of the UK said, in his Report to Parliament earlier this year, "There has, overall, been a widespread feeling   of not being valued or appreciated for their work." A Judicial Attitude Survey among salaried judges in England and Wales courts and UK tribunals was conducted in September 2014.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Only 4% thought that they were valued and 96% thought that they were not valued by the media.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Only 4% thought that they were valued by the media.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, almost every single one felt not valued and two-thirds thought that they were less respected.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Half of all the judges saw media representation of judges, 56%; and public misunderstanding of the judiciary was 59% as factors driving the changes.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A public perception survey on the UK criminal justice system was conducted in 2013/2014.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And 64% of the respondents were confident of the fairness of the criminal justice system in the UK, meaning 36% did not say that they were confident.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One-third did not say they were confident in the fairness of the system.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And only 31% of the respondents were confident that the courts were effective at giving punishments which fit the crime.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have the highest regard for the higher courts of the UK and the quality of their best lawyers.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are truly amongst the best in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But it does not follow that how the UK government has treated its judges, how it has paid them, how it has resourced them, how it has protected the judiciary as an institution, offers a good model for us to follow.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Judiciary is properly resourced, and we try and retain the prestige of our Judiciary.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is quite astonishing that the British High Commission should give us advice to follow what Britain did.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Britain found itself in an untenable position, a difficult situation.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Their judiciary did not have the standing or respect that it used to enjoy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And then the Law Commission reluctantly recommended that the offence of scandalising the courts be abolished because the situation had gotten to a stage where it was no longer possible to reverse what was happening.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Did the British High Commission know these facts when the advice was offered?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the High Commission knew the facts, then that does not speak well of them, because we are not in the position Britain found itself in.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have given Members the survey data on how our Courts are viewed by our public.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are in a healthy, good, enviable position.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we are not about to shortchange our Judiciary.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are not struggling or swimming against the tide of public opinion as Britain was.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the British High Commission did not know these facts and yet gave the advice, then, again, it does not speak too well.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Before I leave this point, I should deal with one other point.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Everyone knows the best British lawyers are extremely good and their senior judges are exceptional, world-class.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And their system is known for its independence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Then why is it that their judges feel undervalued, under attack, and public confidence is not exceptionally high?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A significant part of the reason is because of the media.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It wields an undue amount of power in Britain, with significant influence on politics and finds profit in attacking the judiciary and has been allowed to attack the judiciary.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The uncomfortably close relationship between the British media and the political leaders and its impact on public policies are widely acknowledged and criticised.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In one of his final speeches as British Prime Minister, Mr Tony Blair lamented that in the UK, and I quote, the "relationship between public life and media is now damaged in a manner that requires repair.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The damage saps the country's confidence and self-belief; it undermines its assessment of itself, its institutions; and above all, it reduces our capacity to take the right decisions, in the right spirit for our future." In 2011, the British Government commissioned the Leveson Inquiry.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That Inquiry said, "The evidence clearly demonstrates that, over the last 30 to 35 years and probably much longer, the political parties of UK national Government and of UK official Opposition, have had or developed too close a relationship with the press in a way which has not been in the public interest".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That politicians considered that their control of the supply of news and information to the public, in return for the hope of favourable treatment by sections of the press, was "necessary to counteract the attempts of some sections of the press to discredit their motives and distort the policies that they seek to promote".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When he was asked why he was so opposed to the European Union in an interview a few years ago, Murdoch famously said: "That's easy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When I go into Downing Street they do what I say; when I go to Brussels they take no notice." There have been numerous commentaries examining the impact of corrosive criticism by the British media on the public perception of institutions.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is a fairly straightforward point: you let the media attack institutions, including the judiciary, over time, trust in the institutions will erode.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A judiciary which is not protected, which is underpaid and which feels undervalued, over time, it will take its toll.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Britain may be able to face all of this and still be successful.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Dutch Prime Minister this year described Britain as a country that "has collapsed – politically, economically, monetarily and constitutionally".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Britain may well succeed despite reaching a situation where it was described in these terms.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is one of the largest economies in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It has the capacity to deal with the issues it faces and succeed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But for us, if we are ever in a situation where a serious person like the Dutch Prime Minister describes us as a collapsed state, we will truly be in trouble.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think I have been clear to Members why I reject the British approach.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And as for the British High Commissioner, I think he should spend some time studying the facts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This Bill alone is not going to make it happen.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But it is a part of the total picture.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Currently, the common law imposes no limits on punishing an offender for committing contempt of Court, although certain statutory limits are imposed on the State Courts.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is for the Courts to determine the appropriate punishment, after taking into account all the facts of the case before them, for example, how serious or aggravated the conduct was.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These maximum punishments apply to all types of contempt, including those who fail to comply with Court orders, some of which involve corporate defendants and potentially large sums of monies.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, they could have moved millions of dollars in contempt of Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The maximum punishments are not far off from punishments which have previously been meted out by our Courts for contempt.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The prescribed maximum punishment must take into account the possibility of even more egregious acts of contempt being brought before our Courts and also repeated contempt – second time, third time, fourth time.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As I said earlier, former Chief Justice Chan Sek Keong had also requested that the statute set out the limits.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is similar to criminal law in Singapore in other contexts as well.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Contemptuous conduct can occur outside of Singapore, but its harmful effects on the administration of justice may be felt in Singapore and by Singaporeans, for example, if a plaintiff decides to wage a media campaign against the defendant from outside Singapore, when proceedings are ongoing in Singapore, or where one party prevents a witness from travelling to Singapore to give evidence in a Singapore trial.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But, of course, all the limbs as to what amounts to contempt must be satisfied.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Where contemptuous articles are published through the Internet, contempt of Court is committed if it is accessed by a member of the public in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Under clause 19 of the Bill, for publications taking place outside Singapore, the publisher is not guilty of contempt if he or she did not know and had no reason to believe that the publication would be seen or heard by members of the public in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Contempt of Court is also committed where the disobedience or failure to comply with our Court's order occurred outside Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The key test is whether the contemptuous act directly interferes with, obstructs or poses a real risk of interference with or obstruction of the administration of justice in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There is no reason why a person should be permitted to circumvent contempt laws by publishing contemptuous statement or performing contemptuous acts overseas if the intention is to impact in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Third, there is a need to provide a quick remedy that would allow contemptuous material to be removed before widespread harm is caused.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The AG must be satisfied that it would be in the public interest to do so before making such an application.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The High Court will grant leave if, prima facie, the identity of the publisher and the contemptuous nature of the material are shown.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The author of the statement or the publisher can apply to the High Court to set aside or vary the directions.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the publisher takes the view that it is not contemptuous, he can apply to Court to set aside the direction or order.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the Court takes the view that the material is not contemptuous after hearing the publisher, the publisher would be free to publish the material without restriction.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A person, who is not the author, but otherwise has control over a publication would not be guilty of committing scandalising contempt or sub judice contempt, if the publication or distribution was done without that person's authority, consent or knowledge; and if that person had acted with due care or caution.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: To avoid ambiguity, the Bill provides that the Act, when passed, will prevail over any rules of the common law that would be inconsistent with the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: However, there is a need to maintain flexibility for the Courts to develop other areas of laws on contempt, especially given the pace of change, so the Courts have that power.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This Bill will help maintain the integrity of the system, and I have taken some care to deal with every clause and all the different arguments and explained our rationale.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, I know Members have come with pre-prepared speeches but I would ask that, in the light of the explanations that I have given, Members may want to consider your speeches and deal with the points I have raised as well.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That will make the response much more efficient.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Over the past week, we celebrated Singapore's 51st birthday and the Olympic accomplishments of our athletes, including that of Joseph Isaac Schooling.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have been blessed with relative peace in our country.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During the State Visit to Washington DC, many people shared with me that current affairs, globally, show that the world is becoming increasingly uncertain and the course of events even more unpredictable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is not confined to a particular country but is the general tenor of many regions around the world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Almost on a daily basis, we are engulfed by news of shootings, bombings, terrorist attacks and political unrest.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Against such a capricious backdrop, how can Singapore retain its unicorn-like uniqueness?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can we maintain this crucial stability as a nation?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must deploy and use a workable formula.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And part of this formula includes strong institutions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our state institutions, also known as Organs of State, are respectable and respected.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The acclaim of our Judiciary within the region, and, if I dare say, its increasing respect in the world, has allowed for the setting up of the SICC.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another natural consequence of the strong rule of law is the growing stature of the SIAC.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are classic examples of the consequence of the strong rule of law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A direct result of such international recognition of our Courts and the application and development of Singapore law through our Courts have encouraged economic investments in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: International and Singapore investors have the assurance that their contractual rights will be recognised and adjudicated upon by an impartial, incorruptible set of Courts in Singapore, which is largely viewed as competent.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The rule of law in Singapore is alive and vital for stability.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But let us drill down on what this actually means.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It means that the Singapore Court must be given the space and intellectual autonomy to apply Parliament's intentions which reflect the collective will of the people in the cases that are heard before it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, the Court's reputation and how it is perceived by members of the public are critical.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because if untruths are allowed to flourish, which run the risk of impugning the reputation of an Organ of State, such as the Judiciary, this will jeopardise the ability of the Courts to act as effective adjudicators of rights, whether to private citizens or bodies corporate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our Judiciary plays a key role in the stability that Singapore enjoys.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Do we want to preserve that by putting in measures to protect the institution, which is the intention of this Bill, or do we want to weaken that by allowing statements that risk the Judiciary's ability to dispense and be seen to dispense with justice?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That is the hard junction that we are at.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What we decide today will impact this stability we hold dear.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What this Bill seeks to do, from a macro point, is to introduce legal mechanisms to preserve the already excellent reputation of the Singapore Courts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is why I stand, Mdm Speaker, in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A strong Judiciary, through which justice is not just done but also seen to be done, is of central importance for Singapore to reach SG 100.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With that set out, let me now drill down into certain elements of the Bill which, in my view, are justifiable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is a form of contempt of Court.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When faced with scandalous allegations, it is difficult for judges to rebut them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some have commented that the inability to scandalise the Judiciary infringes freedom of speech.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The law of contempt does not disallow criticisms of judgments.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But, if you have something fair to say in criticism of the judgment, you can.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While this argument may be well-meaning, I am afraid I am unable to agree with it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What is the difference between a risk and a real risk?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I read and reread paragraph 10 of the Petition.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It seems that the formula proposed is to insert real before risk.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A risk, by itself, already means that there is a possibility that the Courts will be scandalised.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That we do not want an untruthful allegation or a scandalous misrepresentation to be made against the Court, such as to risk the ill-repute of the institution, is the intent of this law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And as I have said above, we are starting from high ground; the Courts are already well-regarded as impartial adjudicators of rights.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: All we seek to do is to preserve this.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And even though we are preserving and protecting the repute of the institution, an individual can still offer fair criticism of judgments.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, criminal statutes, generally, do not have qualifiers, such as "real".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And another quote, "Whoever causes the death of any person by doing any rash or negligent act amounting to culpable homicide, shall be punished" under section 304A, Penal Code, Chapter 224.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The statutes are clear in this way, without qualifiers, such as "real".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to ensure that we can act fast if there is a risk.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If there is no risk, then there would be no danger of lowering public confidence in our Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But if there is a risk, then do we want arguments on whether it is a real risk or a risk to hinder effective action under the statute?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After all, cases still have to proceed when untruthful statements are swirling around.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Cases do not halt just because it receives fair or unfair attention.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And at this stage, I declare my interest as a practising advocate in Singapore at the Singapore Bar.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Do we want to be distracted by every current question, such as real risk or risk, especially when time is of the essence?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I started my legal career as a judicial officer working with exceptionally capable and committed judges of the High Court and State Courts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At a young age, it was impressed on us by exemplary senior judges, like Justice Chao Hick Tin, Judge of Appeal, that our decisions had to be well thought through, fair, impartial, thorough and even in language.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Justice Chao still possesses these traits and still sits on the Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This protection should be reciprocated by the Courts in the form of impartial and well-considered judgments of even language.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For this, role models, such as Justice Chao, Judge of Appeal, are key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: You see, a little doubt can go a long way to cause irreparable damage.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hypothetically, there may be a situation in which the risk of that publication is bordering on, what may be called a small risk.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But this insidious publication is part of a host of other publications released at almost a daily rate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The cumulative effect may lead to the last straw on the camel's back that shakes the public's confidence in our judicial system.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would we want such a situation in which the intention of this Bill cannot be borne to fruition?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The point I am making here is that we would never be able to predict what this last straw is and when it will be placed on the camel's back.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The answer to this question would most probably differ even among a small group of well-meaning commentators.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just as "little strokes fell great oaks", let us not allow cumulative small risks to cause the public's confidence in our Courts to fall.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I conclude by going back to my point on the contempt of scandalising the Court.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An institution upheld for the stature it holds or a blanket licence for people to denigrate it?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Do we want to cultivate an ecosystem which allows risks but not real risks to scandalise the judiciary?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As acknowledged by the Ministry, our existing law on contempt of Court already protects the due administration of Justice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The law is to be found in case law and it has worked thus far.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have seen no evidence of the law's inadequacy.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While codification of the contempt laws is not of itself objectionable, there are several things abhorrent about this Bill and the way it is being bulldozed through Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My party colleagues will elaborate further on our objections.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For my part, I will focus on two aspects: (a) the Government's inaccurate characterisation of the Bill as largely business as usual; and (b) the self-serving nature of the Bill for the Government and, in particular, how the Bill is designed to protect and empower the Minister himself.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In my view, the Government had not been frank in its characterisation of the Bill as nothing more than a consolidation of the existing law and a crystallisation of processes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) press release on 11 July, "The Bill will consolidate the key elements of the law of contempt into statute.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The boundaries of contempt, what is permissible or not permissible to do or say, will not change".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is a clear change from the existing case law, which is that, it is only contempt if such statement or act poses a real risk that the administration of justice will be undermined.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
