text: The test of real risk has been explained by the Court of Appeal in the Alan Shadrake case to mean that the risk must not be remote or fanciful.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have not read anything that says that the Court of Appeal or any Court has recommended that it needs more protection in this regard.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, I am wondering whether the Minister in his own words is "chasing shadows".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After all, scandalising contempt is still being retained in our laws so long as there is a real risk that public confidence in the Judiciary will be undermined.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A new power is given to the AG to issue a non-publication direction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under this new power, the AG may issue such a direction to a person to stop publishing something if the AG is satisfied that it is in the public interest to do so.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Disturbingly, the Police are also being brought in to investigate contempt allegations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry has also been insisting that stakeholders were actively consulted on the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What does active consultation mean and who are these stakeholders?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Bill will impact not just selected stakeholders like judges, lawyers or bloggers, but society at large.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As pointed out by the Court of Appeal in the Alan Shadrake case, the law of contempt operates against a broader legal canvas that touches on freedom of speech which is enshrined under Article 14 of the Constitution as a Fundamental Liberty.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Given how the Bill will impact society as a whole, there should at least have been a proper public consultation before the Bill was tabled in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What I know is that the Bill came up for First Reading on 11 July.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was only the next day, 12 July, that the Bill was put up on the Government feedback portal REACH.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was also only on 12 July that the Law Society sent out an email asking Council and all Standing Committees of the Law Society for feedback by 18 July to enable the Minister to prepare his Second Reading speech.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is this what is meant by active consultation, to ask people for their feedback after the Bill has already been tabled in Parliament?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, the Minister gave examples of infectious disease outbreaks and bank runs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But when one looks at the illustrations in the Bill, two recent incidents spring to mind.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To my mind, this is a striking reference to the Minister's utterances on the Benjamin Lim case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Minister had strongly criticised the President of the Law Society for speaking out, but said that public officials like himself, on the other hand, could make statements.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Illustration 2 may refer to the Thaipusam riots in 2015 where three men were charged with disruptive behaviour.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Minister again made comments on what the three accused persons had allegedly done while their criminal cases were still pending.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He told the media that one of the men had assaulted the Police and all three had used vulgarities, matters which were then yet to be decided by the Courts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, would the Minister confirm the exception in clause 3(4) is really meant to benefit himself?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But the existing law is clear that the Government is subject to the contempt of Court laws.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One of the only reported cases of sub judice contempt was in 1967.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That case was brought by a student activist Mr Lau Swee Soong against the then Minister of the Interior and Defence Dr Goh Keng Swee.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Dr Goh had issued a press release after a student demonstration on 4 November 1966 and Mr Lau unsuccessfully brought an application for contempt of Court against Dr Goh.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even though Mr Lau's application was dismissed by the Court, Justice Choor Singh was careful to state in his judgment that: "It does not follow that a statement made or issued by a Government Minister can never constitute contempt of Court or that the Government Minister should never be punished for contempt of Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I come now to my next point – the increased powers given to the AG under the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the face of it, the AG can only issue the non-publication direction with the leave of the High Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But disturbingly, the High Court's hands have been tied in this matter.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This lack of discretion given to the Court is in sharp contrast with the discretion given to the AG under clause 13(1) to commence proceedings.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry said that there was active consultation on the Bill with stakeholders including the Judiciary.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Did the Judiciary concur with the wording of clause 13(7)?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, in the case of Public Prosecutor vs Au Wai Pang or Alex Au, Mr Au was cleared of contempt for one of the two statements which the AG began contempt proceedings against him for.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Bill provides that the Police may now investigate potential offences under the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clauses 22 to 24 enable the Police to arrest suspects, take statements and use all powers available to it as it would when investigating an arrestable case under the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In recent years, we have been talking so much about the heavy workload and manpower shortages faced by the Police.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Why are we getting them involved in yet another non-core function when they should be focusing on keeping us safe from rockets from Batam?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: More fundamentally, what are Singaporeans supposed to expect?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will the Police knock on your door for a critical comment that you have just posted on Facebook?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Recently, seven to eight Police Officers turned up at a house of an activist being investigated for breaches of the Parliamentary Elections Act for postings on a personal Facebook page.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a spectacle, if applied to this Bill, will clearly have a chilling effect on public discourse.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If this law had been in place when the Law Society President had spoken about the Benjamin Lim case, we might have seen a spectacle of the Police raiding his home for possible offences relating to sub judice contempt.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Are we not using a sledgehammer to kill an ant?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would be intimidating not just to persons on the receiving end of such investigations but to society at large.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The upshot of reducing the role of the Courts and vesting draconian powers in the Executive is to leave Singaporeans at the mercy of administration discretion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We would be one step closer to being a Police state.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Are we an exceptional nation when we say that our professionally trained judges need to be protected from public opinion?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Are we an exceptional nation by making Government officials exempt from contempt laws?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To me, these are matters we should be ashamed of.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By all means, uphold respect for the administration of justice, but laws which protect the ruling elites at the expense of ordinary Singaporeans have no place in this House.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, thank you for the opportunity to speak on such an important Bill.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To a newcomer like me, today is very special.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Earlier on, we witnessed a very exciting and passionate moment.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: However now, we are debating a Bill which hit many nerves.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: First of all, I do believe that the Bill can, to a certain degree, ensure that the Court's orders are obeyed and providing legal sanctions on individuals who disrupt and impede the administration of justice.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As such, the terminology used in the Bill must be clarified so that we collectively understand them and adhere to the Bill to the letter of the law.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, as the Bill states, it serves to protect the people across all strata of society, be they large corporations and people of standing, or the common man on the street.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This is specifically in relation to sub judice and contempt by scandalising the Court.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Before I elaborate on my reasons for saying so, I would like to express my gratitude to the Minister for providing some clarification on what has remained fundamentally unchanged in this codification of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I will discuss these areas of concern in my speech and hope the Minister can clarify.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill has a wide-ranging impact on the public's ability to legitimately comment, discuss and debate on matters of public interest that affect each and all our lives.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The Government's encouragement of active citizenry has seen more Singaporeans becoming increasingly involved and interested in public matters, with individuals and civil societies alike stepping up to raise – if not address – concerns.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In many ways, their commitment to the betterment of society has helped the Government make some very good decisions in the interest of the public.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, the petition that I have submitted on the Bill highlights the concerns of many Singaporeans with regard to how it will impact their lives and society at large.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I will give some examples to demonstrate how the public has benefited from discussions on pending Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Dominic Lee was a full-time National Serviceman who passed away in a training accident due to an allergic reaction.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, I wish to highlight Acting Minister Ng Chee Meng's Ministerial Statement on this matter.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister acknowledged that questions and concerns were raised as to whether Benjamin's school's protocol was adequate in protecting Benjamin.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister also said that such public concern was fully understandable, but had chosen not to respond earlier because a Coroner's inquiry was about to be held; in other words, comments made on this case could be considered sub judice.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The public concern over Benjamin Lim's case led to the Police reviewing their procedures when interviewing young persons.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Again, Mdm Speaker, as the Minister has himself acknowledged, there is value in permitting the public to discuss pending Court matters or, in this case, when there is a Coroner's inquiry.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, I believe it to be necessary for the public to have the right to comment on such cases, especially when the issues intimately affect their lives.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Although the purpose of the Bill is not to ban discussion on pending cases except for that which might potentially be sub judice, unfortunately, a combination of factors might lead the public to err on the side of caution by not commenting on cases at all.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: These include the severe punishment, the overreach of who may be liable for contempt, the vague definition of sub judice – which I will touch on later – and AGC's ability to obtain a Court order to require a takedown of potentially sub judice publications.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: One issue with the Bill is that it prescribes severe and disproportionate punishment for contempt of Court.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In contrast, a person who has voluntarily caused hurt or caused another person to be unconscious is only punishable for no more than two years in prison and/or a fine of not up to $5,000.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Such high penalties might deter the public from participating in discussion or be imposed on members of the public who participated unknowingly.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Under what circumstance would a person be liable for contempt?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: According to the Bill, a person is said to have "published" if he merely disseminates or communicates by oral, visual or electronic means a potentially contemptuous matter to a member of the public.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To put it simply, if I shared a potentially contemptuous publication on Facebook, even if I had no intention to interfere with the course of any pending Court proceedings, I could potentially be prosecuted.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Such a wide definition of the term "publication" further gives the public reason not to comment on pending Court cases.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore Court has only had one instance where it contemplated the legal requirement for sub judice to be made out.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I would like the Minister to clarify what would pose real risk to, or prejudice and be sub judice to the whole proceeding.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To give an example, if a relative of the accused were to write on her Facebook page, "I hope the truth will be revealed", will she be in contempt of Court?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It would seem like a very reasonable post to make.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Or what if the post said, "I don't agree with how the case is being handled"?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As an art-maker, in 2014, I made a work entitled "Both Sides now", dealing with end-of-life issues.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: During the same period, the case of Yang Yin, the ex-tour guide accused of misappropriating $1.1million from a wealthy Singaporean widow, made the news.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As part of my project, we held public talks at outdoor spaces, one of which was on wills and the Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA).

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Inevitably, given how the case was topical, there were comments made by audience members in a public space.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Would their comments have been considered sub judice?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The same question can be asked of humorists Mr Brown, Mr Miyagi and the satirical site, Newnation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They are often quick to comment on issues of the day with hilarious effect, which many Singaporeans enjoy.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: These light-hearted moments, sometimes on current Court cases, do nothing more than raise a chuckle.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Will our local funnymen be in contempt of Court for their sense of humour?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In the Dominique Lee and Benjamin Lim cases that I have mentioned, public concern and outcry over the pending Court cases have encouraged the authorities to re-examine internal procedures and policy.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We, as a nation, would be much poorer off without such discussions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: What is of particular concern is that the order may be granted even though such publications may not actually pose a "real risk" in undermining the public confidence of the administration of justice.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The publications are in contempt as long as the AG deems them so at first sight.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, the AG does not have to inform the person to whom the order is directed at before it applies to the Court.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The affected person, therefore, cannot be present at the Court application.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: One would have thought that the Court would have benefited if it was able to hear from both parties as to whether the takedown order should be granted.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: From what I know, the accused should only be tried by evidence led in Court, and not by extrajudicial evidence.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The sub judice rule also seeks to prevent witnesses from being influenced by extrajudicial material.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: However, witnesses' testimonies are not the only evidence which the Courts have before them.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Evidence given by witnesses must also be tested against the body of objective documentary evidence tendered in Court.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, the Court has the discretion to evaluate the veracity of the evidence before relying on it.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Given the above, it is not clear how compelling the justification of the sub judice rule is, especially when we have an eminently qualified Judiciary that can ensure that evidence which have a greater prejudicial rather than probative value is not admitted at trial.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Another point I would like to raise is the exception given to the Government.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is for this very reason that we are debating this Bill, so that it reinforces public trust in the Court and protect its integrity.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, new evidence might later emerge, either through the trial or through other sources, which the Government may not be privy to at the time of making the statement.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This might render previous accounts given by the Government to be factually inaccurate.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In such cases, would such an account of wrong facts, even if it was done in good faith, not be prejudicial to the parties involved in the Court proceedings?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, I would like to touch on the part on scandalising the Court.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: For example, would what was allowed before be no longer allowed in the future?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We have had clear instances where public debate is beneficial and constructive in that it guides institutions to relook at existing regulations and revise them accordingly for the betterment of all.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It would, therefore, be helpful for the public and the House to have clear definitions of what the public can or cannot do in its own interest.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, the queries I have raised are not unique.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: They are shared by various members of the public via petitions, conversations, dialogues with bloggers, civil society people and art makers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Such discourses are essential in any healthy democracy.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We need to protect the public space that allows us to seek clarifications and make suggestions towards the improvement of our institutions, modus operandi and guidelines which, in themselves, are meant to protect public interests.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: A meaningful dialogue goes a long way to help us understand complex issues better and, especially one that holds so much interest at stake.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, we ought to think about how to make all these conversations that we have here reach out to the public.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am reminded of a game that I have played in theatre called the "Trust Circle" whereby there will be a person in the centre with people around him.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As he falls, the people will hold him up.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is a game that is about trust.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But what is important as we learn through this game is that the people around them must have the responsibility to take care of the person in the middle, but the person in the middle must be able to have the tenacity and the strength to take the robustness of this exercise.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And that will only help to build a very robust and strong Judiciary system.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It provides greater clarity and certainty on what constitutes contempt.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It will also ensure that Court orders are obeyed, that the right to a fair trial is preserved for everyone, and that the trust in the Judiciary is not eroded by attacks on its integrity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: On the whole, it is a positive step forward.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, I have two observations and suggestions to make, not to reduce its weight and its punitive effect, but to further augment and strengthen the Bill and for it to stretch further.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I say this with conviction because I was representing one of our unions in IAC two years ago where the Court had given a judgment for the union.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In that case, the employer who was supposed to make due payment failed to do so despite reminders and dragged their feet for an extended period of time, to the detriment of the workers affected.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In the same vein, the sanctions offered in this new Bill also create a greater deterrent effect on those who contemplate to ignore the judgment and not treat it seriously.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I submit we can do more to better align what is provided in the Industrial Relations Act to address contempt of Court with what is provided in this Bill, which will become law once passed.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I have sounded the tripartite partners prior to this Sitting and they are supportive of this.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In this respect, I urge more be done to strengthen and streamline the enforcement of tribunal orders and judgments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As an ordinary person who relies on the law to protect my family, I find this proposed law casts too large and fearful a shadow on the whole of Singapore and diminishes my sense of security for my family.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, the timing for this Bill is most unfortunate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister was careful to point out that he consulted AGC to make sure he would not be in sub judice contempt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He also said that the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) would study how the Police and other institutions could respond in future to such allegations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this Bill the response that he had promised?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If it is, how can this Bill claim to merely codify common law rules when it is coming so quick on the heels of what the Minister had said in Parliament just five months ago?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If it is, is the response not too fast, too furious, too hasty, given that the Benjamin Lim case is still pending?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If it is, should such a Bill with all its terrifying consequences not be given an airing for public debate?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Surely, given the potentially far-reaching impact of the Bill, all Singaporeans should be considered stakeholders to be widely consulted, and not just selected legal and judicial fraternities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Reading this Bill as an ordinary person sends a chill down my spine.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I sincerely hope this is not the intended effect of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is also not clear what is meant by, I quote, "a real risk of prejudice to or interference with, the course of any Court proceeding that is pending".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, a young person has died in an event following the acts of public officials, and members of the public empathise with the parents' loss.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would I, as the father in question, be risking sub judice contempt if I asked fair questions about the event?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would I, as a concerned member of the public, be risking sub judice contempt if I questioned and criticise the authorities in good faith?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is clearly referring to the Benjamin Lim case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Conversely then, would concerned members of the public who made the so-called allegations in the first place be in sub judice contempt?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What if the so-called allegations were questions concerning the factual matrix of the events and circumstances, for example, how many public officials were involved, what they were wearing, what they did, what they said, when they did what and said what and where?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These so-called allegations are not known to be inaccurate and incorrect until the Government clarifies the facts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Surely, by common sense then, when the facts are unclear on a case of great public interest, members of the public who question the factual matrix in good faith should not be in sub judice contempt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, why does the Government get a special clause giving it blanket immunity and a special illustration in this regard?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why not the ordinary citizens, the vast majority of whom would only question the authorities on facts in good faith?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, a corresponding illustration should state "a statement by a person questioning or asking for clarifications on the facts of the events and circumstances relating to and leading up to the death of persons (such as the acts of public officials when a Coroner's inquiry into the person's death is pending) made in good faith on a case of public interest is not contempt of Court by virtue that such a statement constitutes fair criticism." In fact, if this law is not to create a deathly silence among good citizens, then this Bill should include clarifying clauses with illustrations about what constitutes fair criticism and, therefore, is not sub judice contempt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By stating in opaque and ominous terms what the members of the public cannot say without stating what we can say, and, conversely, by giving the Government complete discretion that its officers can say almost anything, this law will scare the public into silence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Scaring the citizens into silence is not something any Government should want because it breeds an inner contempt for the authorities and our public institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the long run, this inner contempt, unexpressed thus inarticulate, invalid but uncorrected, will undermine trust of the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead of protecting the Police and other public institutions, as intended, this will ironically erode the foundation that gives the Police and other public institutions their strength: the trust of the people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Trust is a two-way street and is built on the two-way traffic of communication that is often messy but ultimately coordinated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am an ordinary citizen who would like to be able to express fair criticism and fair comment on events of public interest that concern me.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I was just sworn into this House when the public furore surrounding the Benjamin Lim case reached its crescendo in the online public sphere.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, some unfair allegations were made, but a lot more fair questions and comments were also made, because everyone was concerned, parents were concerned. "What if it were my son?" "It could have been my son." "How could this have happened?" As a new Non-Constituency Member of Parliament still overawed by the moment of being elected, I saw Members of Parliament on both sides of the House picking up on the public concerns and posing questions to the Ministers for Education and Home Affairs, some with emotions audible in their voices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I saw the Ministers answering the questions factually and respectfully.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I saw appreciation when the Ministers promised review of processes of investigation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After the Parliamentary session, I saw the Singaporean public, ever so rational, calming down.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For some, they were willing to submit their doubts to the truth-finding process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For others, questions remained and they continued to ask questions, but in more measured tones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yes, there were those who were still unhappy, their prejudgment unshakeable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But on the whole, Singaporeans clarified their doubts and affirmed their trust in the Police and our public institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The point I am trying to make here is that this episode saw beneficial communication between the citizens and the Government, and trust was affirmed, perhaps even deepened as a result.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would be a grave mistake to see the episode as an attack on the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government needs no protection; there was no attack.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Imagine if this Bill were already law, in January this year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: AGC and MHA would have had its hands full trying to warn members of the public genuinely concerned with the Benjamin Lim case that they were risking sub judice contempt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Otherwise rational citizens would get angry seeing the authorities trying to silence the affected parents and other concerned members of the public.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Courts may issue a gag order, often to protect persons involved in the case and the judicial process, but it is a different matter when the Executive does the same, because it would be perceived as protecting itself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fair criticisms, fair questions, fair comments would all be driven underground.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Members of Parliament would find it difficult to adequately represent people in their attempts to raise the issue in the House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government would have missed out on the perfect opportunity to clarify the facts and affirm its relationship of trust with the people through the most important communicative platform in the country: Parliament.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fewer allegations and misrepresentations might surface, many people would be technically free of sub judice contempt, but the doubts and questions, uncorrected and unasked, would have rotted in people's hearts into unexpressed contempt for the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to talk, take more time to consult the people, talk about it, debate about the contents and rework it from the vantage point of ordinary citizens who seek the security of the law for their families.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to make three points at the outset in agreement with what the Minister has said and one point in connection with what I have just heard from various Members.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In agreement, let me say that ECHR jurisprudence should have no place in this Bill and I do not think anyone who studies ECHR, like some of us do, would think that it should have any place in how this Bill is devised.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we should not heed the advice of any foreign government, especially a foreign High Commission settled in Singapore, as to what any Bill or domestic law in Singapore should say.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The third point, Madam, is that I do not see a background ominousness about this Bill.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I do not see a nefarious purpose to this Bill.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What I and other fellow Nominated Members of Parliament seek are further clarifications.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: When I say there is nothing nefarious behind the Bill, I say this because I have seen and I was in Court at the time in 2010 when the former Chief Justice, whom the Minister mentioned, said that there was a purpose and a need for this Bill.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In his words, he said this: "Laymen and many lawyers have to read the case law or the textbooks to find out what the law of contempt is.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Further, punishments for contempt of Court are unlimited and at the discretion of the judges… Putting the law in a statutory form will allow potential offenders to know what they can be in for." There is a legitimate interest in ensuring that the public, people at-large, know what they are in for.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And that is an important purpose to have any statute codified in a Bill and then in law.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill sets out, in one place, what the law of contempt of Court entails, the powers of the Courts and the limits on punishment that can be meted out.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I agree with the Minister that we must guard against scandalous attacks on the Judiciary.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And allow me to quote Justice Quentin Loh in Alan Shadrake vs AG.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He said that when we determine whether there is contempt of Court, Courts must bear in mind that in Singapore, "we are a small, crowded, multiracial and multi-religious nation where information travels widely and where social tensions, if developed and brought to boil, will propagate." Not only is Justice Loh's statement good law in Singapore because of that decision, it is also good sense.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I have a feeling that today's Hansard might be closely parsed and interpreted by the Bench and the Bar for time to come.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: My concerns relate to three areas where the Bill departs from or tweaks Singapore law as it now stands.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We are looking at Singapore law when I make these statements.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: When former Chief Justice Chan Sek Keong said we have to allow potential offenders to know what they can be in for, I look at clauses 3 and 13 and I would like to ensure that we get as much clarification as we can, even if that means restating what has been said before, so that we ensure that the Parliamentary record is absolutely correct, so that it can be interpreted by the Courts as we intend it to be interpreted.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The public should know the bright line that exists between the two types of speech: permissible speech which any member of public can say, which would not be contempt, as opposed to what would amount to contempt of Court.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Lawyers and judges might understand this, but, in Parliament, I think we have a duty to ensure the public-at-large will also understand it because of what we say here today.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Most importantly, for me, if I may disclose my interest as a teacher and as a law professor who teaches Year 1 students legal method and system and legal writing, there is an interest for young students to know what they can or cannot say, for them not to imagine that there is a "gag" on any objective critique that they can make.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In short, it says that an international publication that impugns the Court and poses a risk that public confidence in the administration of justice would be undermined, would be contempt.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that other Members, such as Mr Christopher de Souza has mentioned and made a good point as to whether there is really a proper distinction between "real risk" and "risk", or is it just a semantic distinction.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I would say that if we were talking about it in the layman's sense, there will be no difference.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But if we were looking at it in a Court of law, judges would legitimately find the differences between the two.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Justice Andrew Phang, Judge of Appeal in the Alan Shadrake case at the Court of Appeal said this: "In applying   test, the Court must avoid either extreme on the legal spectrum, that is, either finding that contempt has been established whether there is only a remote or fanciful possibility that public confidence is undermined on one hand; or finding that contempt has been established only in the most serious situations on the other." Permit me, therefore, Madam, to ask the Minister the following points of clarifications, if I may.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Again, the real risk test is Singapore law as it currently stands for scandalising the Court.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I say this, for a moment as a lawyer, because I ask whether, looking from case law, we are moving to the "inherent tendency" test of years past.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is my assumption that the Minister does not think that is the case.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But, Madam, I would like a clarification as to what is the standard that should be applied for risk of scandalising the Court.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Next, Madam, if I may move to clause 3(1)(b) which deals with sub judice.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I ask this question because this particular word "prejudges", in the context of "sub judice", as to what would then ultimately be prejudice or real risk of prejudice or interference, comes, in my mind, from The Sunday Times case that the Minister spoke about earlier today.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: That is not a case that is followed in England or in any other Commonwealth law jurisdiction nor in Singapore.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And I would assume that it is not an attempt for us to go back to that case because, under that case, the prejudgement principle states that prejudgement of a pending or ongoing case would amount to contempt regardless of how reasoned and temperate any criticism was.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This looks at a point that has been spoken about today in the House and it is specifically with reference to clause 3(4) as to what the Government believes.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I note that this is a special exception for the Government.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And in my view, a special exception for the Government while new to Singapore law – it does not exist in common law as far as the Government is concerned in Singapore – that special exception is permissible, but it must be balanced as to what would be then permissible for a member of the public for the purposes of parity.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Ministries should be shielded from unmeritorious contempt of Court proceedings where they speak or make statements in the public interest.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The question that nags my conscience is what happens when Ministries speak beyond the three crucial areas that we have no doubt deserve that protection.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I am talking about public order, public security and public defence.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: For those three areas, there is no question that the Government of the day as a whole, and the Ministries in particular, are best placed to figure what is necessary in the public interest.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If that is the case, what is the recourse that a member of the public or a concerned citizen would have in that context as far as contempt of Court proceedings are concerned?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Under our system of Government, which is based on the Westminster model, the task of being the final arbiter must fall on the Judiciary.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Judges, after all, whom we all respect in this Bill, are entrusted with the task of ensuring that any exercise of state power is done within legal limits.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Courts, in my opinion, Madam, must be the final arbiters and the guardians.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is my impression that the Courts will have a place in actually looking at whether the Government has a belief, which is necessarily in the public interest, and, therefore, can be clothed by a protection or an exception in this Bill.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: That is my understanding, but I would like the Minister's clarification.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I ask this because most recently, in 2015, the current Chief Justice Sundaresh Menon said that the rule of law is the bedrock on which our society has been founded.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And he mentioned again that one of its core ideas is the notion that the power of the state is vested in the various arms of Government and that such power is subject to legal limits.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It would be meaningless to speak of power being limited were there no recourse to determine how and in what circumstances those limits can be exercised.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Judges have the specific task of ensuring, Madam, that the arms of Government are held to the law and, in that sense, the ultimate responsibility for maintaining a system which abides by the rule of law must lie with the Judiciary.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially important in a contempt of Court Bill, where we are talking about the respect for the Court, should they will not be the final arbiter?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If I may ask the Minister to respond specifically to the question I just asked as to whether the Courts can play a role in ensuring there is no excess in terms of what the Government should believe is in the public interest.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Can I also ask, on a pure drafting point: can the Minister confirm that "Government", for the purposes of this clause, meaning when we say the "Government believes" or persons on behalf of the Government, the word "Government" refers to the Executive, that is, the President and the Cabinet Ministers?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I ask this because the Interpretation Act does not define it so.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It defines "Government" as the Government of Singapore, which might not be helpful in this case, because we obviously would not want to look beyond, I would say, the Executive, when we talk about what the "Government believes".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: When we look at this Bill, let me say again that there is certainly a need for the statute.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, there is a need for a Bill, where everything is consolidated in one place.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But I must say that there are two points that I would like to make in conclusion.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is quite clear that the Courts are careful about saying how far the public can speak.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They are careful to say that the judges have no interest in stifling debate.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, if we come from that perspective and we understand that the Judiciary is at the centre of a contempt of Court Bill, and certainly we should look at the most recent decisions, and it has to be strongly emphasised why we would like to depart from them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This concept or doctrine of rule of law is, however, not so straightforward and the manner in which it is interpreted and applied in Singapore has been the subject of considerable debate.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I do not intend to unravel this debate today but would like to highlight the point made by the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew in his oft-quoted speech in 1962 to the University of Singapore Law Society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He highlighted the need to bridge the gulf between the ideal principle and its practice, given our sociological and economic milieu.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He added that the acid test of any legal system is not the greatness nor the grandeur of its ideal concepts, but whether, in fact, it is able to produce order and justice in the relationships between man and man and between man and the state.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is against this setting that I would like to make the following points.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One, our laws and rules need to fit the needs and norms of our society and we should not just follow what is set by other countries without appreciating our norms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Two, the trust and confidence in our legal system, in particular our Judiciary, is exceptionally high and we need to do our utmost to preserve that standing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On my first point, I am of the humble opinion that we should be unabashed with the firm stance taken in relation to contempt of Court, be it by way of disobeying Court orders, sub judice or by scandalising the Court.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Our society places great weight in not saying the wrong things and taking responsibility for what one says.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This means you have to think more about what you want to say and take ownership and responsibility for your words and actions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I do not agree that setting the law on contempt would inhibit robust discussions on matters of public interest.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On the contrary, such laws would promote a more responsible discussion and reporting on matters before the Court at the appropriate time, which is probably after the trial, with the accurate facts when the facts have been determined.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have faith in our people finding the appropriate forum and manner to raise important and relevant issues that can improve our systems.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have always found a way to do it and will continue to do so.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: With regard to my second point, I note that some have raised the argument that if our Judiciary is so well-trusted and respected, then why worry about sub judice and scandalising of the Courts?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is important to emphasise that such high levels of trust cannot be taken for granted.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Even baseless accusations, especially if repeatedly made, can affect people's confidence in the Judiciary.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We cannot allow for the erosion of this confidence.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Minister for Law had earlier taken the time to explain that the proposed provisions do not prohibit fair and even harsh criticisms of decisions or reasoning of the Court.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is one thing to disagree with the decisions but another to allow for space to scandalise the Court.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We may not see it now, but if we stop being less strict about what is said about the integrity, propriety or impartiality of our Courts, perceptions may be created, even if untrue.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If this happens, we will jeopardise the sanctity of judgments issued by the Courts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In the course of my practice, I have seen a significant number of Court orders, especially maintenance orders in the Family Courts, not being obeyed.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I had to console and advise many clients on enforcement proceedings and had to face many clients expressing their disappointment with the paper judgments they received, which may be in their favour but did not improve the situation they were in.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is especially heart-wrenching when it involves issues relating to the children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Significant reforms have been implemented in the Family Courts over the years to improve enforcement of Court orders, with more modes of enforcement of maintenance orders, such as attachment of earnings order.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, we still see judgment debtors who are simply recalcitrant.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In this regard, I would just like to seek a small clarification on one matter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The threat of a fine or imprisonment is a strong deterrent to the recalcitrant debtors but, ultimately, may not lead to the judgment debt being paid.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister publicly remarked after the First Reading of the Bill that it merely crystallises the current legal position on contempt, and I quote, "does not create anything new", unquote.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the drafting of clause 3 suggests this is far from the case.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If it were so, one would have expected specific reference to the "real risk" test as established in the Alan Shadrake judgment to preface the explanatory statement covering clause 3.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, clause 3(1)(b)(i) on sub judice contempt, on a plain reading, is also open to interpretation and is hardly determinative.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A broad reading of the clause with the conjunction "or" suggests that an individual could be guilty of sub judice contempt by publishing something that prejudges pending Court proceedings, by, firstly, prejudicing; secondly, interfering with; or thirdly, posing a real risk of prejudice or interference with that proceeding.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does this not potentially create different thresholds for sub judice contempt, especially since there is a dearth of Singapore case law on this matter?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It also leaves room for the Courts to potentially introduce a test other than the "real risk" test, such as the inherent tendency test which has been summarily rejected by the Court of Appeal, albeit in cases of scandalising contempt but not sub judice contempt.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Should the Minister argue that it would depend on each case, does the Minister not agree that leaving it open-ended would give the Government significant powers to alter the balance between freedom of speech and the administration of justice to its whim and fancy?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At best, it would only serve to confuse the public and does nothing to educate the layman about what qualifies as sub judice contempt.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In reality, it will shrink the common space for discussion on matters of public interest as it is typical of human behaviour to be safe rather than sorry.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That alone makes this Bill bad law, negating its very purpose.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In his remarks to the media shortly after the First Reading of this Bill, the Minister raised the recent case of the two-year-old toddler Daniel who was abused by his caregivers before he sadly passed away.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister correctly observed that many people were angered by the facts of the case, and the Minister queried, in such circumstances, whether a defendant would get a free trial.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Interestingly, the Minister conceded that the judge, the facilitator in chief, in ensuring a fair trial, may not be influenced, but instead the witnesses and the whole environment may be prejudiced or influenced.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, has such a doubt ever been raised in the Singapore context where our Judiciary was so helpless as to be unable to oversee a fair trial and to assess the veracity of the evidence of witnesses?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Under the current legislation, it can be argued that many Singaporeans would have conceivably been in contempt when the City Harvest trial was going on, but did their comments compromise a fair trial?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Coming back to the toddler's case, what actually happened and how fast did public anger blow over?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Were witnesses influenced in spite of the negative feedback?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Most importantly, did Daniel's parents not have a fair trial?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To quote the Minister, has the situation "gone out of control" in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In reality, there are benefits in allowing the public to comment on cases pending before the Courts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, in the recent Benjamin Lim case, no reasonable person would argue that the Coroner would not have been able to rule fairly and this is a testament to the standing of the judicial service, legal service also, which is already held in high esteem, not just locally but internationally as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the Benjamin Lim case, it was the very feedback and concerns raised by the public that contributed to a review of Police procedures involving young people and minors before the case was concluded.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For most lay Singaporeans, the reality is that criticising policies and facts central to a pending case will inevitably overlap to varying degrees.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That is the very nature of public communication and, for the common man, it is not always easy to neatly differentiate the two.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Surely, there is a place for fair comment and criticism of pending cases, and it does not necessarily follow that freedom of speech has to suffer as a result.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The near absence of case law on this matter in our legal history provides the strongest evidence of this.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even our judges, in whom we have so much respect, are prevented by law from refusing to grant leave should a judge deem the prima facie standard of proof to be too low and not in correspondence with the public interest on a particular case.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the Government, through the AG could conceivably abuse the law by virtue of the unclear and highly interpretative words, such as "prejudge" in clause 13, and suggestions of a test with a lower burden of proof than the "real risk" test which mirrors the identical problematic drafting in clause 3.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This vagueness suggests a clear and present danger for civil liberties should the Government decide to interpret the law strictly, as drafted, to muzzle alternative voices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Proceeding on this clause will not only compromise trust between the Government and the people in the long run, but between the people and the Police as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At this stage, Mdm Speaker, it is useful to review the Government's record on civil liberties over the past few years in particular.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 2013, when Parliament passed the Protection against Harassment Bill, the Government canvassed many justifiable reasons for the passage of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many were legitimate, such as protecting individuals and public servants from "indecent, threatening, abusive, insulting words or behaviour".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One would have expected sexual harassment, stalking, bullying in schools to be brought to task under the law as predicted and in step with the tone of public consultation of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But shortly after the Protection from Harassment Bill was passed into law, it was the Government that used the Act to claim harassment from a member of public in a dispute over a mere patent.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is instructive to recall that during the Second Reading of the Protection from Harassment Bill, the Minister was silent about the Protection from Harassment Act envisaging the Government as a plaintiff.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To then turn around and sue individuals was a completely unexpected use of the Act by the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And if suing an individual was not enough, the Government then proceeded to sue an online news site under the same law.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Earlier this year, the Government proposed and passed amendments to the Government Proceedings Act that allowed the Government to claim costs for more than two legal officers from a plaintiff knowing that the Government has limitless resources to hire the most expensive lawyers and an entire army of civil servants and legal service officers behind it to defend any suit.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister in-charge did not even address why it was amending clause 9 of the Government Proceedings Act until Ms Sylvia Lim brought it to the attention of the Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This seemingly innocuous amendment would inevitably cause an individual to think twice about taking on the Government because of the highly prohibitive costs involved.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is especially the case for Bills like the Administration of Justice Bill which give the Government maximum scope of action.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In this vein, there are other pieces of legislation over the years that directly impact freedom of speech, too, and which have been amended to give the Government greater powers, such as the amendments to the Public Entertainments and Meetings Act of 2014, the Broadcasting (Class Licence) Notification of 2013 and, of course, the Public Order Bill of 2009.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Upon a closer analysis, it is increasingly clear that the Government's recent record on civil liberties mirrors what was known in the heyday of the Cold War as "salami tactics", only that the Singapore version is slightly different and a tad more sophisticated, with the curtailing of civil liberties occurring incrementally, bit by bit, or slice by slice, one law at a time – all of which appear justifiable and innocuous when analysed in isolation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Taken together, however, they portend a clear and consistent ability of the Government to control public discourse, fair comment and criticism, should the Government choose to up the ante to tighten its stranglehold on public discourse.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Viewed in totality, the Government's approach gives it significant powers to strike fear in the hearts of ordinary citizens.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Minister commented on a recent civil case where the High Court imposed an imprisonment of eight months.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would appear that the common law is working fine.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It does not matter whether they are teenagers or 20-somethings, conservatives or liberals, religious or irreligious, pro- or anti-establishment, politically active or apathetic.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Though the range of emotions and points they raised differed widely, the common ground of our youths' concerns usually boiled down to a perception that this Bill was telling them to "sit down and shut up" when it came to discussion of ongoing affairs of public interest.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I have found two groups of reactions worthy of close consideration.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: One is from a minority section of youths and the other is from the larger majority of youths.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There is a small but significant group of youths who are active participants in the world of online socio-political discussions.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some of them are active creators of online social political content, others are more like active conduits of the content.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They do not create but they actively consume, share and comment on socio-political content instead.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This group has a remarkably strong interest in national affairs, and I say "remarkably" because, honestly, it is not yet the norm for the average young Singaporean to think deeply about national affairs.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They are our brightest young writers, editors, journalists, activists, artists and creatives.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They are also our most opinionated students in political science, communications, law and other humanities.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They are also a group that fundamentally cares.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: These young people actually heard about the passing of this Bill and bothered to read up something about it and they do have a strong emotional reaction to it because they can see themselves or someone they know and respect, possibly impacted by it.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It may be tempting to judge this whole group of youths as cynics of the establishment who are totally prejudiced against any possibility that this law has any good in it.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And, certainly, some will quite happily live up to that stereotype.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But even so, that should not prejudice us against what they have to say, for it is also an exercise of our own impartiality and desire for justice that we lean into their anger to hear what needs to be heard, clarify what must be clarified and even change what must be changed.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Anger is an off-putting emotion for many of us.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But when we see an angry person, we should pay attention, especially when we disagree because anger is always a revelation of what that person loves.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Without love, there is no anger, there is only indifference.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When we listen into anger, we are listening into what someone cares most deeply about and what they most long to protect, and some of these youths are angry about the Bill because they, too, care about protecting the common man and about protecting Singapore.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They resent what they perceive as an unjust imbalance between the protection of institutional versus individual interests in this Bill.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The quarrel this group of young people have with that clause is not about the reality that a responsible Government must step in from time to time to set the record straight in the face of inaccurate public allegations that are prejudicing an ongoing Court case and that the Government representative should be protected.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They are not naively asking for a free pass to be given to irresponsible individuals to say whatever damaging things they want to say about ongoing cases.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: From a layman's reading, that line feels unfair and can be interpreted as the Government placing itself above judicial reproach.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Their fears are largely founded upon the uncertainties of who exactly is that "Government" in the sentence who is acting as the final arbiter in determining what constitutes "public interest".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Is it the Executive, Legislative or Judiciary branch of the system?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I can empathise with the Government's perspective that figuring out what is necessary in the public interest is complex territory that, frankly, not everyone is equally fit to navigate.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It demands expertise on every level – rigorous intelligence, deep domain knowledge, empathy for stakeholders and just the sheer damn courage to do the right and just thing, whatever critics may say.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is not something a random guy on the street can do; it is also what we expect our highest elected officials in power to do.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, why not just give them the space and the trust to do their job?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But it is deeply frustrating to these youths that the Government seems to be insisting that they are the one and only trustworthy arbiter of what is "public interest".

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What some of the angriest young people are asking is worth hearing and clarifying.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Their questions sound like this: "But what if the guy in the Government gets it wrong?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Isn't it always a possibility that those in power will get what is in the "public interest" wrong some of the time?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And if one of us, regular guys, can see it and want to point it out to them, should we not get the same space to do so as well without fear of being labelled as the enemy of the Court or, worse, the enemy of the state?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And would it be so hard to believe I want the best for my country as much as they do?" The trouble about "public interest" is that there never is just one public interest but many equally good competing public interests.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is always a hard choice to prioritise one public interest over another, and a thinking people will occasionally dispute that choice.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It would be helpful if the Minister could articulate what is the best recourse then for these young people to handle a situation where they vehemently disagree with the Government's interpretation of what constitutes "public interest" in an ongoing issue.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Unless we imagine that only youths uncomfortable with parts of this Bill are the angry, anti-establishment ones, I must point out that there are also some moderates and pro-establishment youths in this group as well.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because of their active participation in socio-political discussions online, even youths not predisposed to distrust the Government feel some low-level of anxiety over the uncertainties in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Even after they read it – and some of these youths are legally trained – they are still uncertain about how easy it will be for them to commit sub judice.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They do not know when exactly their comments cross over from safe to being a risk.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I will now move on to the reactions of the majority of young people I spoke to.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Most young Singaporeans I talked to are actually completely unaware that this Bill is being passed and even when I made them aware of it and explained it, they still felt emotionally detached from it.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They range from either completely indifferent or just feeling at peace with the very same issues that so deeply angered or worried the first group.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When I asked them why they were not getting worked up like their peers, their answers varied.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some said public affairs were just not interesting or relevant enough to be part of their daily online conversations anyway.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some assumed they were just never going to be types who could say anything important, controversial or consequential online.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And some joked that they never questioned anything because they did not want to put in effort to think that hard and that they trusted the people in the Government to do the thinking for them.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: What is curious about this second group is that when I finally asked them whether the passage of this Bill would change the way they spoke online, they all said something casually along the lines of "Aiyah, no big deal, just play safe and don't talk about such things lor.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Get into trouble for what?" And this is precisely why I felt I have to speak up on this Bill.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I shared them to say both groups of young people exist and both groups' reactions must matter to us because they are telling us something important about the future electorate.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Their silence may not be a sign of approval but of apathy, not a sign of consent but of conditioning.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Any law that limits free speech, for better or for worse, will have short-term and long-term cultural impact, sometimes unpredictably so.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, as a result, the public conversation on race and religion is still underdeveloped.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Any law that limits free speech will have complicated side effects on the maturity level of public discourse.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Already, we can hear how the Bill, as it is currently languaged, is being interpreted by some as a despairing signal to sit down and shut up.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It may not have been the Ministry's intended message or mission at all.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But it is clearly one of the complex outcomes that has already emerged that ought to be addressed.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Minister, broadly speaking, I support the spirit of your Bill.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I see the big picture you are driving at.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I share your conviction that trust in the Judiciary must be protected, the integrity of the Court process must be kept and our reputation for rule of law is what makes us exceptional in the world.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: That reputation undergirds the prosperity of our country and should never be casually undermined by absolutist ideals about free speech.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And I am all for safeguarding our country against the culture of contempt as well.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I reiterate the need to give people a space for their anger and protect their right to express that anger on things of public interest.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But contempt is not something I support because it is distinctly and dangerously different from anger.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is anger that has been allowed to fester, anger gone sour.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Anger, at its heart, is still founded upon a desire to protect.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But contempt crosses the line into a desire to destroy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Anger can drive us to right a wrong, but contempt drives us to just want to be proven right above all things, above all people.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: An angry person can still respect the one he disagrees with as his equal.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But a contemptuous person will always denigrate those who disagree with him and see them as forever and always beneath him.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Contempt does cross a thin red line, to do many injustices in the name of justice.
