speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We must never agree to allow words of contempt to flourish freely.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The people who most love justice can be the most angry of people.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Those of us who love justice, who know the passion of righteous anger must be most watchful that we do not allow ourselves to tip into the prideful pit of self-righteous contempt because contempt is the fastest killer of trust and greatest ruin of relationships.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In contempt, there will never be compromise, collaboration nor space for solutions across the divide that actually moves the course of justice forward for us all.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I agree with the Minister that nobody, regardless of how justified they believe they are, should be allowed to spread malicious lies, especially under the pretense of free speech, just to run down innocent people, undermine valued institutions or make money online through clickbait articles.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: People can only speak freely when there is safety, and safety is always founded upon constraints.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We freely choose to put limits upon ourselves to make a space for others to be free and we expect that same favour to be done for us.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Like freedom, justice flourishes only when everybody accepts certain limitations on their rights and certain expansions of their responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But this rule must be seen to apply to individuals as much as the institutions of power meant to oversee them.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I still seek amendments for this Bill because I see phrases within it that create uncertainty in a layman's mind, perhaps unnecessarily so, around the Bill's intentions in this regard.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I will close my speech restating three requests.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I apologise to the Minister in advance for having to use Singlish.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is a language of their heart and they are the audience I most want your answers to travel to.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Number two, following on from question one, some young people are suspicious about that clause I just mentioned because they see it as an example of the Executive branch of Government trying to place itself above the Judiciary's reproach and they worry that there is no check-and-balance in the system.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister address their worries directly and clarify where in this Bill or elsewhere in the law are the assurances that this is not the case?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, would the Minister be able to "double confirm" for them that this is not a situation of "ownself check ownself"?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The philosopher Mengzi observed that in dealing with a small state, a large state ought to use magnanimity; and when in dealing with a large state, a small state ought to use wisdom.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is an age-old advice that can inform the dealings between any smaller and larger entity.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Including this exception for public affairs discussion can be a much clearer communication of the Bill's intent to protect the common man as well as the Judiciary.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is a gesture of magnanimity that speaks volumes and, with all the right constraints, could encourage wisdom.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: There is always going to be a fundamental asymmetry in the relationship between the individual citizen and the larger institutions meant to protect its interests.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The inherent imbalance in power provokes a natural level of uncertainty and, thus, fear.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I believe this Government understands intimately the inherent struggle of the small to communicate with the big because that is what it has dealt on the international level every day for 50 years when far older, greater and bigger countries get perplexed and even insulted at why a small annoying red dot like ours keeps insisting on a place at the negotiating table and having a say in larger matters that seem, in their large perspective, to be beyond our size and, thus, understanding.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But the smaller must always speak up as an expression of our dignity, a fight for our interests and an assertion of our passion for the right of self-rule.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We are small in the world, but we are here and we will not go unheard and unnoticed.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This is true for our country Singapore and it is a spirit that rings true, too, for every citizen who shares their Government's fight to call this place "home".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I would like to share with this House some grave concerns I have about this Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the case of Alan Shadrake, the Court of Appeal rejected the "inherent tendency" test and accepted the "real risk" test.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And let me just quote a very helpful analysis from Prof Gary Chan in his article in the Oxford University Commonwealth Law Journal, and I quote, "According to the Court of Appeal, real risk does not mean 'remote possibility'.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is also not equivalent to 'clear and present danger' or 'serious or grave risk'.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Significantly, the Court of Appeal disagreed with the High Court's description of real risk as any degree of risk above de minimis level, including 'a small likelihood'.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To me, it seems to be everything that the Court of Appeal has said about what a real risk test should not be.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not be departing from the learned analysis and decision of our Court of Appeal.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This clause provides for the possibility of a person who "prejudges an issue in a Court proceeding that is pending and such prejudgment prejudices, interferes with or poses a real risk of prejudice to or interference with the course of any Court proceeding that is pending".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This test of prejudgment in this clause goes against developments in the common law world.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the UK and Australia, such a prejudgment test or principle has been rejected as being too restrictive to free speech.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If introduced in Singapore, it also infringes on our constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression in Article 14 of our Constitution.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am also concerned with explanation (2) in clause 3 which, in effect, meant that when considering what is capable or "prejudicing or interfering with or posing a real risk or prejudice to and interference with any pending Court proceedings", the fact that the proceedings are heard by professional judges is irrelevant.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, there can be a finding of real risk of prejudice even if, in actual fact, no competent judge would be affected by what was said.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Professional judges, unlike juries, should and will not be easily prejudiced by comments made publicly or in the media.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I thought that was what the earlier People's Action Party Government under Mr Lee Kuan Yew had sought to achieve when they did away with juries.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The effect of the proposed law is this: subject to prosecutorial discretion, no one else can say anything even if there may be public interest or other legitimate reasons.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In contrast, the Government has a complete and unquestionable right to do so.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What if a Government spokesperson decides to say it not in the public interest but in the narrow interest of the ruling party?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What if the Government is wrong in its belief or the spokesperson makes a mistake even honest mistake, but to the detriment of some poor individual?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The clause does not provide any protection or remedy to persons who may be prejudiced by such comments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It does not even allow the Courts to disagree or to rule on whether the Government was right or wrong.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is potentially unjust and capable of being abused.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is and ought to be a shared space for everyone in this country including individual citizens and civil society groups.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The test must be an objective one allowing anyone who speaks in the interest of the public.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And even if the Government insists on giving itself the sole right to comment, which I do not agree with anyway, it should, at least, allow an objective test here.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let the Courts decide, in the event of any complaints by any individual, whether the Government's comments were correct or made in good faith.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the State, Family or Youth Courts, the maximum punishment to be prescribed are 12 months' imprisonment and a fine of $20,000.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Alan Shadrake's case, the Court of Appeal noted that it was the "worst case of scandalising contempt that has hitherto come before the Singapore Courts" and yet the Courts saw fit to affirm the sentence given by the trial judge in the High Court, which was a fine of $20,000 and imprisonment of six weeks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2008, Gopalan Nair was convicted of insulting a High Court judge by his comments on a defamation case involving the Singapore Democratic Party and the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew in his blog when he said that the judge "was throughout prostituting herself during the entire proceedings by being nothing more than an employee of Mr Lee Kuan Yew and his son, and carrying out their orders".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the case of Attorney-General vs Hertzberg Daniel and others, a fine of $25,000 was awarded.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is definitely no mere codification of existing common law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The maximum sentences are way above current sentencing practices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Current arrestable offences include offences like unlawful assembly or rioting, affray, rape, theft, robbery, use of criminal force on a person with intent to outrage modesty, voluntarily causing grievous hurt and so on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no risk to the physical safety of the public.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If this House were to allow such provisions, the effect, whether intended or not, will be to intimidate not just potential accused persons under this Bill, but also to cast fear on the public in respect of their right to criticise or comment in both public and private discussions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Clause 13(1) has also allowed the AG to direct an individual to refrain from publishing any matter or take down publications that could potentially be in contempt.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will be a new procedure which is currently not available.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The AG is not required to inform this individual that he has applied for a Court order for non-publication.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The individual concerned will only find out once the order has been granted and served on him.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He cannot, therefore, be present in Court to make submissions to the judge before the order is granted.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He can only apply to the Court after the order has been granted and served on him to have the order set aside.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This process is complex and costly, especially to lay people.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The failure to comply with the order is a criminal offence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More than that, it will also be an arrestable offence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why does the Government wish to bar the defendant from attending the hearing of the AG's application?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What harm will it do to the AG's case if it is a justifiable one to start with?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why does the Government wish to shut out the defendant's defences completely at the onset?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, by shutting out the defendant before a decision is reached, this is a violation of an individual's right to a fair hearing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the Government wishes to criminalise acts of contempt of Court by such a procedure, then, by such provisions, the defendant must be given the right to defend himself at the hearing of the application.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have full confidence in our judges that they can make the appropriate decision after hearing the merits of each party's case.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill's provision for the defendant to have to set aside the order cannot be equated with the defendant's right to defend his case at the time of application by the Government.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It was never his application and he had no notice of the hearing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, by forbidding him to attend the hearing of the application where the burden of proof rests with the Government and requiring the defendant to apply to set aside the order, the Bill has cleverly and effectively reversed the burden to the defendant to discharge the order.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This requirement is just too low and easy for the AG.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we are codifying this as part of criminal law, why do we not apply the criminal procedures' standard of proof of "beyond reasonable doubt"?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And prima facie is still below the civil standard of proof of balance of probability, which, accordingly to this Bill, is the burden the defendant has to overcome when he applies to set aside the order.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, bizarrely, the defendant ends up having a higher standard of proof.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, why not "prima facie" for the defendant?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister has also said that it is a "crystallisation of the law".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But this Bill goes far, far beyond mere codification and consolidation of the present common law on contempt of Court.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My party colleagues in this House have also raised other issues.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If this Bill is passed, our contempt of Court law will become needlessly draconian without necessarily enhancing respect for the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Bill, if passed, creates a huge shadow of fear hanging over Singaporeans who may otherwise have justified opinions on certain topical issues, where the handling by the Government or public body has been subject to criticism or controversy, like what we saw in the case of Benjamin Lim, which actually created awareness among Singaporeans of how Police interviews of a juvenile person are conducted and, in fact, generated positive discussion of how the procedure can be improved upon.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government does not necessarily need to view such incidents in a totally negative way and react by clamping down on comments and discussion on the basis of ongoing investigations but should look at the positive lessons that it can learn from.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us not bring our country a step backward.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Any effort to raise the public's confidence in our judicial system and Court proceedings as well as to ensure individual responsibility and accountability for remarks made through publications or any other avenues to scandalise any party/individual is very much supported.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The question is: will the same treatment apply to Industrial Arbitration Court orders?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: These include fair and accurate reporting of Court proceedings or disobeying Court order due to the honest and reasonable failure to understand the obligations under the Court order.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Should the AG act in discretion of the law, how will this discretion be exercised and is it too wide-ranging a discretion?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Does it leave too much room for interpretation?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How to prove if the motives are proper or improper?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: When can a person comment on a case if it is not concluded and if at all a person can do so, even if there is validity in his grounds to raise concern?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Some cases take more than a year to conclude and, if this is so, does it mean that a person or netizens can only comment on the case strictly after the case is concluded?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If there is a genuine complaint against the judge while the case is proceeding, is there any other channel available to raise this concern or to deal with it?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, to provide clarity on the scope of this law for the public, that is, the people, it is important that the people have to be made aware and be educated so that they may act more responsibly and be accountable for what they comment on and not fall foul of contempt of Court.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, in so doing, it poses an unsatisfactory and problematic solution to a non-existent problem and it generates grave dangers to the freedom of speech that is part and parcel of our Singaporean way of life and is enshrined in Article 14 of our Constitution.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: By creating the potential for abuse of the excessive powers that this Bill confers on the Government, allowing the government of the day to initiate investigations as a means to chill, stifle and, ultimately, strangle debate on matters of public concern while reserving for itself the right to comment on such cases.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First of all, I would like to address the fundamental necessity of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All legislation exists to fill a gap to address the real issue in such a way as to generate improved outcomes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In this case, MinLaw has stated that the Bill primarily seeks to consolidate common law on the subject of contempt of Court.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There has not been a rash of cases that make administration of the common law position on contempt of Court difficult.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is the necessity for this Bill, why legislate and why now?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To cite some unrelated but illustrative examples, the Government has refrained from legislating a quantum on retrenchment benefits into the Employment Act.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It has refrained from legislating penalties for discriminatory hiring and human resource practices by employers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do not argue that such a risk cannot exist by definition, but the Government needs to make the case that the risk justifies such an extreme measure.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If, indeed, such a law were necessary, surely, it is not time-sensitive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, I would like to ask why there was not more widespread consultation, both within the legal fraternity and among the wider public, before this Bill was tabled for First Reading.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As my colleagues have argued, why was a Green Paper not tabled in Parliament, given the very grave issues at stake?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other jurisdictions, before significant changes to important legislation are tabled, law commissions are convened to seek public feedback and advise government and parliament on the best approach to take.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Surely, a Bill that substantially affects the constitutional right to free speech under Article 14 deserves much more public consideration and debate than has been thus far accorded to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, on the offence of sub judice, what are the urgency and necessity for this Bill in this regard?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our cases are decided by professional judges rather than juries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is our confidence in our judges so weak as to suppose they cannot disentangle fact from misinformation and, hence, need to be protected from public statements about their ongoing cases?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Surely, our judges are well-trained in the rules of what constitutes relevant evidence to be admitted and considered by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the concern is with witnesses and experts being influenced by published misinformation, is not the Court process designed so as to elicit the finding of fact, disentangled from the undue influence of misinformation?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For instance, under cross-examination, the subjective can and should be distinguished and differentiated from the objective in any eye-witness testimony.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More specifically, have there been concrete cases of witnesses and experts being unduly influenced by published misinformation to such an extent as to generate a real risk to which this Bill is a response?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In recent years, Mdm Speaker, we have seen many sensational cases which have drawn heated public debate and discussion online and offline, such as the trial of the former head of the Central Narcotics Bureau, Mr Ng Boon Gay, the trial of former law professor Tey Tsun Hang, the trial of the members of City Harvest Church, Little India Riot Commission of Inquiry.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Have there been any specific examples or complaints of witnesses not stepping forward or tailoring their testimony as a result of public pressure?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If not, why the impetus for this Bill?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If there are such cases, I urge the Minister to share such concrete cases under the protection here of parliamentary privilege so that the Singapore public can better understand what circumstances have provoked the tabling of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I note that the Minister for Law, in his speech, did not talk about any other country that seems to be moving in the direction that the Government plans to move here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This underlines the need for the Government to explain why it is opting to move aggressively in this direction.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, the Government's exception clause set out in section 3(4) also creates a real risk of Government abuse, as my colleagues have argued.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Or, in theory once again, consecutive investigations on trivial charges or technical infractions could be launched to keep the matter permanently off-limits to public discussion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An unscrupulous government could use the provisions of this law to suppress public discussion of its failings or wrongdoings in every platform, forum and institution in Singapore other than Parliament itself.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It could be argued that under current common law the Government could do this anyway, so the Bill does not change anything.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I would like to speak about the penalties which the Bill prescribes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In particular, I fear that the $100,000 figure will attract undue attention and become fixed in the public's mind as the liability one must be prepared to pay if a citizen wants to express his or her opinion on a matter of public interest that could potentially be subject to the contempt of Court law.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, as my colleagues have argued, this maximum cap is not aligned with past precedents.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other fines have ranged from $500 to $10,000.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The result for our democracy from the passage of this Bill and the attendant publicity could well be that no one who does not have $100,000 in cash to spare will dare speak up about any issue where there is even the slightest risk or perceived risk of prosecution under this law.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What does that mean for our democratic society, for the voices and contribution to public debate and consensus formation by Singaporeans with limited means?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a climate of high income inequality, do we really want to deepen the view that free speech is only something that the rich can afford?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Bill has certainly received a great deal of attention and I am speaking today to offer my views from the perspective of someone who has spent a few years in the media industry.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I feel that the Bill is an important one because it helps to avoid situations where an accused person may be put on trial by the media.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a particularly relevant issue today, especially with the advent of social media and citizen journalism.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, Snapchat, blogs – many Singaporeans use these platforms to share their views and engage on social issues of the day.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The pervasiveness of media outlets is, of course, a double-edged sword.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Wider access brings with it wider responsibilities, of course, for debate in a civilised and productive manner.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is certainly no laughing matter when a person is on trial facing criminal charges, or if he or she is embroiled in a civil case before the Courts.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a rule that our mainstream media tends to observe strictly, with reporting on Court cases being limited to factual representations until such Court proceedings have come to an end.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, with the proliferation of different types of media platforms, journalism is no longer the preserve of trained reporters.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we have heard from my colleague, Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin, more people are able to air their views and share their thoughts and debate issues.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I feel that, sometimes, they do so perhaps with less of a sense of what constitutes professional and proper publication for public consumption.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am no lawyer and would leave the technical legal points to my learned colleagues.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am, nevertheless, aware that one argument against sub judice laws is that they are irrelevant in a country like Singapore, as we do not have a jury system.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The thinking here is that judges should be impartial enough to consider a case without being influenced by any extraneous material.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I have full confidence in the quality of our Judges and in our Judiciary, I would like to take a different perspective to consider the wider effects of a trial by media.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Consider such a situation that is set out in Illustration 2 listed in clause 3(1) of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The illustration refers to a situation where an Internet news site might claim to have "discovered" the identity of an unknown assailant while a criminal case for assault is still under investigation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this type of case, the consequences of factual misrepresentation in the media would be severe.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a fair outcome for both the accused and the victim and, in my view, is consistent with the basic principle that a person is innocent until proven guilty in a Court of law.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Intense media speculation may also affect witnesses and colour their evidence when they take the stand.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Going back to Illustration 2 in clause 3(1) of the Bill, if the Internet news site had been allowed to run amok with its unprofessional reporting, the accused's name would have been dragged through the mud, regardless of the outcome of the Court case, and on the basis of probably inaccurate information.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If the accused were then to be acquitted, this would be a pyrrhic victory, indeed, as he may well have been vilified in the press, long before the delivery of the verdict.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And even if no actual prejudice is caused to the outcome of the Court proceedings, the damage done to the individual's and, indeed, their families' reputation, psychological well-being and privacy may be irreversible.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To this end, I would seek the following clarifications from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In particular, how will this Bill affect the current reporting practices of the mainstream media and alternative media?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, concerns have been raised that the Bill will affect the coverage of activist campaigns related to ongoing Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will such advocacy be considered as "interfering with" or being "prejudicial to" Court proceedings, as mentioned in clause 3 of the Bill?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is also important as it ensures that both mainstream and alternative media are held to similar reporting standards when covering ongoing cases.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As someone who has been involved with the media industry for more than 20 years, I am heartened that these changes will help our media scene raise its standards and avoid descending into sensationalism and tabloid journalism.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, Madam, I conclude my speech in support of this Bill.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In any civilised society, it prevents the rule of the jungle, the rule of the predator, the rule of the bully.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It prevents the rule of inequality, as other Members have raised.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, a wife, abused by her husband, now seeking divorce, safety, maintenance for the children.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It protects a young family who have lost their breadwinner, now seeking compensation from the employer.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It protects the Pioneer Generation uncle who worked hard all his life, saved up all his life but was cheated out of his retirement savings by unscrupulous businessmen.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The rule of law is also about social norms.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Whether we, as a people, believe that all should be equal before the law; whether we, as a society, believe that the Courts should be the final arbiter of disputes; whether we respect due process and the decisions of the Courts – even and especially when those decisions might go against us.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When a judge sentences a conman, it is not just the penalty or the prison sentence that sends a message.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is also that the judges are respected and, so, their judgments have moral weight.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This is why it means something in our society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And I am sure both sides of the House will agree on this.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It means something when a judge says that someone is suppressing the truth, is dishonest, is a liar, in cases where there has been impropriety, regardless of what sphere they may be in.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, when we protect the stature of our Courts, it is not just about the judges.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is about justice and protecting justice for Singaporeans from all walks of life.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This is why many Members have spoken about Court judgments needing to be enforced, because, otherwise, they are just words on paper without real impact in the real world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is also why we have to protect against other ways in which justice can be undermined.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Imagine, Mdm Speaker, if this were not the case.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Imagine if a wealthy person were accused of a crime, someone wealthy enough to own significant equity in a newspaper.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What if he used his own privately owned media channel to campaign for his case during the trial?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Or if an accused person had a large social media following, campaigning for an outcome during the trial of the case?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some have argued in this House that sub judice is only relevant to countries with jury trials because judges have professional training and expertise.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But witnesses, Mdm Speaker, are lay persons, too, and even though judges weigh evidence, it matters when witnesses are influenced.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It matters when witnesses are undermined by what happens in the media.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What happens, for example, if photographs of an accused person are widely published in a case where identification is an issue?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Will it make the accused's face seem more familiar in the mind of a witness?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What happens if a witness, after reading the media coverage, starts to believe, "Well, maybe this person I have seen him somewhere before".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Would the witness have second thoughts about what they were going to say if they have been persuaded that everyone else believes a different story because that is what has been published in the media?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Would witnesses be less willing to come forward, if they are afraid of being criticised by a newspaper with readership?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: All it takes is for a website somewhere to publish their identity, home address, phone number, maybe even family photos on Facebook.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It seems like an exercise of the imagination.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And it has been mentioned in real situations, even going back many years.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Australia example above and the issue of witnesses were raised in the Irish Law Reform Commission's 1991 consultation paper.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Real concerns from overseas; real lessons we can learn in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is very understandable when members of the public are concerned about what is happening in a Court case and want to discuss it.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But, as has been said earlier, if our loved one were the victim of a crime, would we not want a fair trial?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Would we not want witnesses to be protected, so they can testify without fear or favour, without their recollections being affected by media coverage?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Or imagine you were wrongly accused of committing a crime and the accuser mobilised a social media network or website to get you a trial-by-media, a guilty conviction in the minds of the public, even though the Court might later find you innocent.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On the one hand, freedom of expression, but we must also be mindful that it does not undermine the right of an accused person to a fair trial.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because when the Courts are diminished, it weakens their ability to protect the weak and the vulnerable.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The idea of "necessity" already exists in the common law of sub judice.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That is why restrictions on public discussion are for a limited time only.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It continues so long as the limit is necessary.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I accept, Mdm Speaker, that there are situations where there may be public alarm or a threat to public safety and the Government may have to put facts out in the public domain.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the era of hybrid warfare, non-conventional threats, it is entirely possible that an attack might be followed by a deliberate campaign to publish false information, to turn Singaporeans against one another.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This will help minimise the risk of affecting an ongoing Coroner or Court inquiry.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And by ensuring interventions are no more than what is necessary, that check and balance will, in turn, further reassure the public's confidence in the system.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But neither must we become free market fundamentalists on this.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As I have said previously in this House, it is quite possible for market failure to occur when there are inadequate constraints on the market.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It can happen in the marketplace of ideas as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is helpful to codify the law of contempt in order to give Singaporeans a better understanding of what actions tantamount to sub judice, disobeying Court orders and scandalising the Courts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The reality of today's society, where there is easy access to virtual soapboxes, is that there will always be individuals who will be irresponsible and hold extreme views.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I support provisions in the Bill to manage media outlets and commentators, some of which are primarily motivated by sensationalism and scandal, rather than the search for the truth.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I, however, would like to raise a few questions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While I understand the need to address inaccurate or incorrect public allegations, however, following the release of a Government statement, is it possible for exemptions to also be made when a member of the public provides a differing but factual description of events and circumstances?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also provide further details on what safeguards will be put in place to ensure that judges are not influenced by the Government statement?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, while the Bill seeks to provide clarity for lawyers, the text in its present form may expose the layperson to risks that they may not fully understand.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this age of social media, where flurries of spontaneous conversations fill the Internet, the layperson may not fully understand where the line is drawn and what he or she cannot say.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Does this also include academic articles or a private Facebook post?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And can the Minister also provide a more detailed description or definition of what is considered "fair criticism"?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are questions relevant to the public which we should have ready answers for.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also propose efforts to raise public awareness in order to help the layperson understand the boundaries of what is legally tolerated and not.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This Bill sets up clarity and certainty on what constitutes contempt.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I welcome this as it sets out boundaries so that people are in the know how far they can go with the laws, without running afoul of them, and the consequences that they have to face if they choose to go against it.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This will also allow people, especially those who previously tended to err on the side of caution, to now speak with confidence and to speak more freely.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In the context of sub judice, I believe that everyone should have a fair trial.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I agree with the majority whose opinion is that the freedom of speech should not lead to "people on trial" being influenced by social media vigilantes' opinions and postings.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This Bill will further strengthen our legal system and the integrity of our Courts.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This Bill is thus timely and in the right direction.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The maximum punishments prescribed in the Bill are appropriately aligned, to be commensurate with the affluence of today and should be sufficiently high enough to be taken by the majority as adequate deterrence.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Under contempt of Court in disobeying Court orders, such as flouting orders on maintenance payments and access to children, this Bill provides a framework for more effective enforcement of Court orders.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Most people believe in the need for effective enforcement of Court orders.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The greater clarity of this Bill will instil greater confidence that the judicial system is able to enforce Court orders effectively, as such, giving the reassurance to the afflicted parties.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The clarity of this Bill will also let people know upfront the consequences of non-compliance.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: After divorce, it is frequent for parties not to comply with Court orders on maintenance and access to children.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The sufferings and pains of the aggrieved divorced parties are hence quite obvious and a solution to ameliorate their difficulties arising from non-payment is necessary.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: There are also many parties who do not take out Court proceedings because taking out proceedings to enforce Court orders can be stressful, time-consuming and costly.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: At my Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS), meeting such afflicted families, usually the female spouses, has always been regular occurrences over the years.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Sad to say, due to the demographic profile of my residents, those afflicted with non-compliance of maintenance payments are usually in dire straits.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: They usually do not have other means to support themselves and their family members.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Often, they have many children, some of whom are still young.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: They usually do not hold jobs or, if they do, they usually get only meagre incomes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, the daily survival needs of their families are in jeopardy.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: We should send a strong signal that disobedience of the administration of justice on purpose will not be tolerated in matrimonial spats.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: All said, the truth is that, very often, social issues are complicated and the Judiciary has to consider all factors before mitigating punishments.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of my MPS cases have complicated family issues.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Some male spouses who came to my MPS told me that they had to flout the maintenance Court orders because of retrenchments; others said they had second families to feed due to subsequent marriages, often with young children as well.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Other male spouses had complained to me at my MPS that their ex-spouses had denied them access to their children, causing them agony.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Some spouses said access orders were breached, as the children themselves did not want to see the other parent after the divorce.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Will they be judged with more understanding and sympathy?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In the case of non-compliance for a male spouse due to inability to pay as the result of more commitments from a second or even third marriage, sending them to jail for non-compliance will certainly disadvantage every member in that person's marriages.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Section 12 does not provide for any other forms of punishment.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Adding a fine on him or sending this defaulter to prison in such an instance may not serve the course of justice at all.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, I would like to seek the Minister's clarification on several concerns.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I find it useful that the Bill seeks to codify the current law on contempt so that members of the public will not have to second-guess what constitutes contempt of Court.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Just as important for the layman, the Bill provides for defences in Part 4 of the Bill and, through this, clarifies what is not contempt.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, clause 14, where scandalising the Court is concerned, reports made to the Chief Justice, the Police or a law enforcement agency concerning a judge's alleged misconduct or corruption is not considered contempt.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These are avenues by which concerns on the Court can be channelled.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Two, where sub judice is concerned, the Bill provides for the defence of persons who are communicating in private or who have no reasons to believe that their content of discussion would be seen or heard by members of the public.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The freedom to seek, receive and impart information and ideas of all kinds is regarded as a human right in international law.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, it is also a human right to be entitled to a fair trial and the presumption of innocence until proven guilty according to the law.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, Madam, whilst I fully respect the need for the freedom of expression, I believe that public discourse must not come at the expense of those who should be presumed innocent until proven guilty, upon completion of Court proceedings.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I refer to the accused parties involved in high-profile cases which may or may not have gained public sympathy, such as Mr Yang Yin, the ex-tourist guide, for alleged misappropriation of monies from an elderly widow; and former chief of Central Narcotics Bureau Mr Ng Boon Gay for alleged corruption and who has since been acquitted.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the case of City Harvest, in which six church leaders were prosecuted for alleged misappropriation of funds, the investigation and trial spanning six years had seen much adverse comments being cast in media and by members of the public in public forums.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some observers were of the opinion that the accused might have already been tried and convicted in the Court of public opinion.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I especially empathise with those with young children who are paying the price of such conduct.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As an American judge once said of unbridled reporting allowed in the name of freedom of speech and expression: that "free speech which is the strength of the nation can be the cause of its destruction".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The first one is on how the Ministry can ensure that freedom of expression is not unnecessarily muzzled whilst upholding the principle of fair trial and innocence of defendants till proven guilty and, in the process, help ensure that the vulnerable in their lives and the lives of the accused are not subject to trials by courts of media and public opinion.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The second clarification is on how the Bill can prevent abuse of the privilege of government, current and future, to exercise its right to comment on matters in the name of public interest; and for the Minister to provide illustrations of the circumstances, beyond SARS and runs on banks, under which this right is exercised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I think that much almost every speaker today agrees on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is a means by which our Courts can assure that its authority is not undermined and act on to prevent those who do so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: As Lord Denning, a very famous British law lord, once said, "The course of justice must not be deflected or interfered with.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It would be useful, first, to understand what is the state of law today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And the Bill sets this out very clearly with added explanations, illustrations and examples as to what amounts to contempt.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: These categories of conduct are no different from the conduct which amounts to contempt in common law as it stands today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: There are three aspects to it and I will cover them very briefly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: First, a person will be liable for contempt if he or she disobeys the orders of the Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This is very straightforward, requires no elaboration and can really brook no dissent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The Petition, in fact, regards all of these objectives as "laudable" and I think that must be correct.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Under our current law, lawyers, academics, laypersons are all free to criticise the outcomes of civil and criminal Court proceedings and decisions: to argue that a judge's reasoning was wrong, to say that the Court has misunderstood or ignored the evidence or placed the wrong weight on evidence, to argue that the Court's sentence in a criminal case was too harsh or too lenient in the circumstances.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: None of these would amount to scandalising, whether under the existing law or in the current Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, in a recent decision by the Court of Appeal, our highest Court, the Court was asked to consider an argument that the Court of Appeal had itself acted improperly in its own previous decision.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I was the counsel in this case and the question which arose was whether there might be reservations in mounting a strong challenge against a decision of the Court of Appeal on the ground that the Court of Appeal has itself acted in breach of fair hearing rules.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In considering such an argument, the learned Chief Justice observed that the Court would, in fact, expect "nothing less" than such a case be pursued with the "utmost force".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: He went on to say, and I quote: "Those who present difficult arguments to the Court with all due vigour but also with all due respect and etiquette that we expect of our officers, have nothing to fear".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, when the hon Member Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan said the Courts are the final arbiter, this is their view.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Our highest Court has made it clear that fierce and vigorous criticism of Court decisions, even those of its own Court of Appeal decisions, they are permitted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And there are clear rules by which this can be done.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This happens, in fact, frequently, and our existing common law rules on contempt of Court already permit all kinds of criticism to be levelled at the decisions of the Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Likewise, under the new Bill, this is no different, and I would ask the Minister simply to confirm this, to quell the disquiet that seems to have been going around this Chamber about what additional measures or additional hurdles this new Bill has put forward.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I now turn to the issue of interference with Court proceedings, whether by publication or by intimidation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The Petition seems to say that because of this that legitimate expression and discussion on public interest will be curtailed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, I would venture to suggest that such statements are alarmist and reveal a fundamental misunderstanding as to what this Bill and the law are all about.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Everyone is entitled to a fair trial – the accused, the victim, their families and the potential witnesses.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This is the law today and this is what the Bill has encapsulated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The real mischief which the existing law on sub judice statements, as codified in the new Bill, seeks to guard against is the prospect of "trial by media" and, as the Minister outlined earlier, the prevention of whipping up of sentiment against or for a particular outcome that a trial is meant to decide on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In the course of my own practice of the law, I have noticed the marked proliferation – as I am sure all of you have – of social media and its effects on, in this case, the administration of justice, in particular, the increasing risk of trial by media.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This is where an individual who is being tried in our Courts is accused, vilified and disparaged in the media or on online platforms which are accessible to many.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Such behaviour is prevalent in other jurisdictions, especially where there are tabloid newspapers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In relation to what has transpired in some overseas jurisdictions, I do not think we need to look beyond some of the highly publicised cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Further ago, we had Michael Jackson's case, and more recently, we had Oscar Pistorius' case, both of which received significant public media attention which, to some extent, relegated and completely overshadowed the actual Court proceedings from start to finish.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: There is no shortage of local examples as well, as some of my colleagues have earlier outlined.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The effects of trial by media on the conduct of a fair trial in our Courts and the effect on an individual's life, and the prospects of that individual's chances and merits at a fair trial cannot be underestimated.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It undermines the presumption of innocence, it could taint or discourage witnesses from coming forward and affect the evidence they give in Court, and puts the judge under unnecessary public pressure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And this can either be real or perceived.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: What is wrong with coming down strongly in this case in favour of a fair trial?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: While prejudicial information may historically have faded with the newspaper print, as well as from our collective memory, as data, it is now processed, archived and is retrievable for very much longer periods of time".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, clause 13 of the Bill, in my view, seeks to address the fresh challenges which the new media poses, whilst at the same time, maintaining the constitutional balance between freedom of speech and the necessary limitations to such freedoms to protect against contempt of Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This has been described as a "new power".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But, even under the current law, it is already open to the AG to obtain a Court order, in appropriate cases, to restrain publication of statements which constitute contempt, including on an ex parte basis, and even before publication.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In this case, I believe the issue is one of balance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: On the one hand, we cannot shut out legitimate public discourse, which I agree is the hallmark of an engaged, active citizenry which we want in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But we also cannot allow a small minority of persons, who may have an agenda to insult, vilify, sensationalise, publish with callous abandon, especially with the Internet being what it is.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Publication, re-posting and sharing occur instantly and, in a few hours, can become viral.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It will be difficult, if not impossible, to completely remove postings, and that is precisely what the UK Law Commission had in mind.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And so, if we are to have any meaning behind our contempt rules, especially as regards the commission of contempt by publication, there has to be some power to stop the publication at source.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: If we agree that acts of contempt are harmful to the public interest, then the AG ought to be empowered to take swift and decisive action to prevent or stop the publication of such material in appropriate cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I accept that there could well be occasions where a Court might subsequently decide that the publication does not actually amount to contempt and sets aside the take-down order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And the burden is on the AG to make an application to obtain ex parte, give full and frank disclosure, disclose all material facts to the Court, which also acts as a safeguard in scrutinising any such application.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: As a starting point, if we accept that our society needs the contempt rules, and that these rules are laudable, then such rules must be capable of enforcement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Again, the power of our Courts to administer punishment for contempt is also not new.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This power is already in our current Supreme Court of Judicature Act and our State Courts Act.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Further, as in the case of Alan Shadrake which has been mentioned earlier provides, our law already allows a sentence of both imprisonment and a fine as punishment for contempt.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And recently, as the Minister mentioned, there has already been a case where a Court has meted out a sentence of up to eight months' imprisonment for failure to comply with a Court order.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: What this Bill does, however, is to prescribe an upper limit on the length of imprisonment and the quantum of the fine.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is important to remember that what the Bill sets out to achieve is to set a  maximum punishment permissible by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This is the case in almost all of our penal statutes; it sets a maximum ceiling but this does not mean, as some speakers in this House seem to suggest, that the maximum will then become the benchmark in all cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Our Courts currently have, and under the Bill will continue to have, the discretion to mete out the sentence to fit the crime, to be appropriate, to be proportionate and to consider the relevant facts in each case of offensive conduct.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Our judges are well-equipped and experienced in this exercise as there are many offences in the Penal Code and others for which there are maximum sentences and which require our judges to exercise their discretion in sentencing every day.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: There is, in fact, a whole body of law just on how that discretion ought to be exercised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is important for the range of punishments to be set out clearly, as some of my colleagues have acknowledged, and for our Courts to then have the discretion to decide within that range.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But really, one cannot apply one case and say that that becomes the standard for another.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is not cut from the same cloth, and so, it is not one size fits all, and the range simply gives our judges the discretion to apply them in the context of the relevant case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This will, indeed, ensure that the most vulnerable amongst us will have proper recourse in the event of non-compliance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And before I leave the point on punishment, quite a number of Members have relied on the disparity in what happened and was meted out in Alan Shadrake being regarded by the Courts as one of the most serious cases of contempt.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The only reason or one of the reasons why the Court of Appeal did not change the sentence in that case was because the Prosecution did not appeal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, it felt that this was what it would be bound by as a punishment given by the High Court.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, it is not tenable to use Alan Shadrake and the example in the Alan Shadrake case to say that we have moved the benchmark and moved the goalpost significantly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: First, because of what has been debated in this House and the seriousness of the matter, could the Minister give some further examples of trial by media and explain the damage which could be caused to ordinary citizens, whether to the accused or otherwise, and how the laws might then apply?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Second, in particular, clause 2(1) which defines "publish" to be dissemination or communication to the "public at large, or to a member of the public".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Could the Minister clarify what does it mean to publish something "to the public at large or a member of the public", and how would this be distinguished from "private" communications?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: That is one of the concerns articulated, especially by the Member Ms Kuik earlier, and I think that is a valid point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: If a group of friends sitting around in a coffee shop decides to discuss the ongoing criminal trial amongst one another, would that be caught by public communication?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We feel that the existing law is sufficient to ensure that those who are held in contempt of Court will be punished accordingly.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: As of now, there is no evidence to show that the law has lost its effect.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The real purpose behind this new Bill on contempt of Court is not to protect the fairness of our judicial system, but it is to deter members of the public from voicing their fair and reasonable views on cases under trial.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, however, it allows Ministers to make a statement on ongoing cases, which could possibly affect the judge's judgment on the trial.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: There is a Chinese saying to describe this situation: only the officials are allowed the freedom to set fire, but the common people are not even permitted to light a lamp.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Yet, if the statement is made by a Government official, particularly a Minister, then it is a different matter altogether.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Clearly, the new Bill will provide the Government and the Ministers with unfettered power.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: A statement, which could be considered as contempt of Court when it comes from a member of the public, becomes completely legal when it comes from the mouth of a Minister, as long as the Government believes that it is in the public interest to do so.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The question is: what is considered to be in the "public interest"?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: There is no clear explanation in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Of course, it is the Government that gets to decide.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: As the saying goes, the (Chinese) character "guan", meaning "government", has two mouths.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: So, even if the ruling party's intention is to protect its own interests, as long as they say it is in the public interest, what can the people do about it?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: That is to say that the ruling party is the sole judge on interpreting what is public interest.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It can also justify the elimination of any dissenting voices, including organisations that oppose it, by accusing them of "not being in the public interest".

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In 1967, there was a contempt of Court case in the High Court.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This was regarding the student riot in November 1966.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The then Minister for the Interior and Defence, Dr Goh Keng Swee, made a press statement, and one student activist sued Dr Goh and accused him of contempt of Court.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Although the High Court eventually acquitted Dr Goh, Justice Choor Singh then made a very clear judgment in principle.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: However, now, Parliament is going to pass this Bill to say that as long as a Government Minister decides that it is in the "public interest", he can make statements without being construed as in contempt of Court, free of any restraint by the Court.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In other words, the Government can define by itself what "public interest" is, and then use this "public interest" as a protection to go beyond the restraints of the law and the Court, and make statements and pass comments freely on ongoing cases.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is very likely to prejudice the trial, seriously interfere with the administration of justice and undermine people's trust in the independence of the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In addition, under this new Bill, as long as the AG feels that any individual or organisation has made a comment in contempt of Court, he can apply to the Court for an order to deal with the person making the comment, while the Court, in the whole process, ends up being reduced to be the administrative assistant of the AG, assisting him to execute his orders.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is a situation where the AG supersedes the Court.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: On 11 July, MinLaw made a statement to say that this Bill is to codify the laws on contempt of Court and there is no change regarding what can be done and what cannot be done.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: However, the real effect, once the Bill is passed, is that Government Ministers' power will override the Court and the Judiciary, allowing them to do whatever they wish according to their own needs and convenience, with no curtailment from the Court.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This Bill is a typical case of "pretending to advance along one path while secretly going along another".

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The WP oppose this Bill because our existing law has already provided rules on keeping administration of justice fair.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This Bill is not only unnecessary, but it is also giving the Government additional powers that it does not have now, to intimidate the people from making fair criticisms on ongoing cases.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: If the Bill is passed, it will result in the gradual erosion of peoples' trust in the Government in future.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 7.20 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 7.05 pm until 7.20 pm.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have heard a wide variety of views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will respond to the issues that have been raised as well as some of the more specific queries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, is the question of timing and motive of the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some suggestions that we are rushing this, that what is the rush, does it have to do with Benjamin Lim, are we chasing shadows and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Former Chief Justice Chan Sek Keong said in an interview five years ago that scurrilous remarks, unless firmly dealt with, would inevitably undermine public confidence in the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Indeed, there was no rush, and this Bill has taken longer precisely because there was no rush.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Otherwise, the other three heads are exactly the same.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The way it is set out is exactly this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have explained numerous times in my opening speech and really the question is whether you accept it or you do not accept it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said it in 2012 and I said it in 2013.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Former Chief Justice Chan Sek Keong said it in 2010.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if you want to put up a conspiracy theory, I think you got to try harder.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The reason we did not push on with this Bill is very simple.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, even in the absence of the Bill, the law is there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is just that it is better for it to be in writing because it is criminal law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is the only criminal law that is not set out in statute.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, at some point, we have to set it out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, all these suggestions of democracy under attack, we are going to restrict freedom of speech, make for fine statements outside if you believe that you can mislead the public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But for a real debate, it does not meet any of the points that I have made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It really raises questions whether the speeches here are meant for a real debate in our First World Parliament or they are made for consumption outside in the belief that the public can be misled.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As for what I said about the Bill when it first came out on 11 July, I have said that the Bill clarifies and crystallises the process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim, I think maybe Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, asked me what sort of consultations were conducted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But underlying it all, the fundamental point to remember is when looking at this Bill tomorrow, Tuesday, assuming the Bill gets passed into Act today, the law is essentially the same.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some processes, additional processes, are there but the law is essentially the same.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I say that and look anybody into the eye and say that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If anyone says that that is not true, tell me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We took into account the feedback received before the First Reading of the Bill and I have to say we made a number of amendments based on the feedback.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As regards what was set out by Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry @ Home (REACH), the article published in REACH invited readers to share their views on the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But a number of consultations had taken place before the First Reading.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang made a fairly impassioned speech but I have to say the entire speech seems to be based on a misunderstanding of what the Bill is all about because everything the Member has said is factually untrue and I will explain why.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Member raised the spectre that ordinary citizens sitting in a coffee shop talking will be charged with contempt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How does ordinary citizens sitting in a coffee shop having a beer and talking about a case pose a real risk of prejudicing any proceedings?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the law yesterday is the same as the law tomorrow, have you seen anyone being charged for sitting in a coffee shop and talking about cases?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we want a debate that engages honestly on the facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
