text: I will tell you when someone sitting in a coffee shop discussing a case could be contempt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you catch hold of a witness, have a beer with him and try and influence or threaten him in a coffee shop, that will be contempt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if you sit with your friends and talk to them about a case, how do you think it impacts on any case?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Low also said that the Government can say whatever it likes and the Courts cannot do anything.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Under our system of law, the Courts are the final arbiters of any provision of the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government has got to act in accordance with the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun, Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin, Assoc Prof Mahdev Mohan and others asked me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What Justice Choor Singh said – if a Minister stands up and speaks about a particular case in a manner calculated to prejudice the proceedings and if he does it in bad faith, then I think he will be committing contempt and the AG will be entitled to commence proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, in real terms, what that sub-clause provides is no different from what is happening today and what has been happening all along.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I told you about bank runs; I told you about hospital incidents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The last hospital incident, there was an inquiry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At that time, it was entirely possible, in fact, Coroner's inquiries were going to take place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Nevertheless, the Government came out and made statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does anyone think that the Government should not make those statements?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Would it be tenable not to say anything?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us say a couple of people get killed in an accident involving a public transport company.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But can the Government wait until then to come out and say what it knows, what has happened, what actions it has taken?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A few people died and nothing is said?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is that the way the Government can function?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This has been going on since time immemorial.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whatever our Minister says, whatever a Government agency says, ultimately, you apply, you look at the clause and you see whether the statement comes within the clause.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This was specifically discussed between us and the Supreme Court and I put that on record.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it makes great buzz when Mr Low says all the people in the coffee shop, they are all now going to commit contempt, ordinary people; whereas the Government can say what it likes; untrue and untrue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a third point Mr Low makes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the whole process, the Courts have become an assistant to the Government; untrue again.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The AG, if he believes that there is contempt committed today, has to apply to charge the person.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That means he says that you have committed an offence and he charges you.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What it says is, you do not have to charge in every single case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Instead of charging, what you do is, you go and apply to the Court, and you try and persuade the Court that there is contempt and the person should take it down.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court decides whether or not AG satisfies the Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if the Court disagrees, it tells the AG, go away.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He serves it on the person who has published.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The person who has published is not happy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He can go back to Court and say this is not contempt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, please, let us not misrepresent the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We can have disagreements on points of principle, judgement calls, but let us not go out and say things which are completely inaccurate about what the Bill does and does not do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng asked me about the Government making statements and whether it is subject to the Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Tan, yes, I think you heard me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leon Perera made an impassioned speech: grave dangers to freedom of speech, rush to legislate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I did not know the Member would consider six years to be a rush to legislate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Substantially affects public debate; are there any cases where witnesses have not come forward?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why did you assume there is a change?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Your entire speech, Mr Perera, with respect, proceeds on a fundamental misunderstanding of what this Bill is about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is your logic: this Bill has been put in to curb freedom of speech, you have rushed it this year, you are trying to curtail freedom and you are trying to do it by stealth and as a result of this, tomorrow, democracy is going to be much poorer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would not say exactly because of that one change.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But other than lawyers, nobody else will argue about "real risk" and "risk" and that relates to a specific narrow area, unless you think that the majority of Singaporeans wish to say every day that our judges are biased.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think it is a fundamentally important area for most people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is very important as a matter of principle, but it is not something which happens on a daily basis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If it did, we will be in trouble, we will be like the British.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are probably a couple of prosecutions a year at most.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I stand corrected but that is the kind of figures we are talking about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Which clause makes a change to the law?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Which clause impacts on your freedom of speech more than it does today?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Which clause affects democracy more than it does today?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Dennis Tan has made the point that we should not depart from what the Court of Appeal has said in the Alan Shadrake case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts, fundamentally, are engaged not in a policy exercise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They do not weigh up the larger social policy considerations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They look very narrowly at case law and say this is the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We, the Legislature here and the Executive, are engaged in a broader policy exercise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said in my opening speech, we are the leading legal centre in this region and we have every possibility of being a clear number one in Asia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have also said how important the rule of law is.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why do we get reputable international judges coming in to sit on our SICC?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why is our SIAC one of the leading centres in the world?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In that context, I said it is a weighing exercise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the one side, it is the integrity of the institution; and on the other side, the need for a very small number of people to say judges are biased, judges are corrupt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When you take that weighing exercise, we are in a better position as a matter of policy to decide what the law ought to be.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if I hear any cogent argument as to how this change from "real risk" to "risk" in the narrow context of accusing judges of bias, of personal misconduct as judges, of corruption – we are not talking about other things; only these sorts of areas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why the right for some people – probably we will end up with two or three in a year – to say that should outweigh our view that by protecting the Judiciary in this way, and without getting into arguments as to whether when I say the judge is a biased swine in public, in a way that makes an impact on people, whether I should be allowed to say, "Well, you know, I said that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does undermine the Judiciary, but you know, it is a risk of undermining but it is not a real risk." Do we want to get into that?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I agree reasonable people can disagree on this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I have put to you why I have taken this approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The points on clause 3(1)(b)(i) again proceed from misunderstanding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the Government exception, why we need the Government exception, I have explained.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If any Member here thinks that we can run our society and our Government without the Government saying anything when major events happen, just because there is potential litigation, I think please stand up and tell me whether that is possible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If two people die on the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) tracks, whether you think it is possible for us to keep quiet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whether if five people die out of a virus outbreak in a hospital, even if we suspect fraud, whether you think we can keep quiet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you think we should, please stand up and tell me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, if there is bad faith, if it is calculated deliberately to prejudice on-going proceedings, the Courts can look at that clause and intervene.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Tan also made the point that the maximum punishments are too high and goes well beyond that in the Alan Shadrake case, and that was a point made by a number of the other Workers' Party Members.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think there is, if I may say so, an unhealthy obsession with one aspect of contempt – scandalising the Court and the Alan Shadrake case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: From our perspective, contempt covers a broad area and there are four different heads that I have referred to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The punishments that are set out in the Bill must be adequate to deal with any of those.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, when it comes to scandalising the Court, yes, the punishments have been a few weeks but when a defaulting husband who does not pay and when he could have paid and he is recalcitrant, the Courts have sentenced him to eight months, which is not very different from what we are providing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us say you have a case where there is an injunction, what is commonly known as a Mareva injunction.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You freeze $100 million and the defendant moves out $50 million, in breach of the Court order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He is brought before the Court and he is charged with contempt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What do you think the penalty ought to be?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And supposing he does it a second time and he moves another $25 million.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What do you think the penalty ought to be?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, move away from this obsession with one provision and look at the totality of contempt and then ask yourself, what should be the maximum punishment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Within that, under the different heads, the Courts will decide what is the appropriate punishments for scandalising the Courts or interfering with the administration of justice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think in the coffee shop case, if you go and threaten a witness and tell him that you are going to break his leg, I think that person should go to jail, but that is my own view.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Tan also had some viewpoints on the process by which the AG can go to Court and get leave of Court to get an order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said this reverses the burden of proof, it is forbidding and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Somebody publishes something, the AG believes that this interferes with current proceedings and may cause serious risk or real risk of prejudice to the administration of justice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has to persuade the Court that he should get an order to get the person to take it down.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If he gets the order, he then serves it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Every lawyer who is in the civil arena will know this is standard operating procedure.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is how lawyers get injunctions and mandatory orders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is nothing unique; this is bread and butter stuff.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is lost in these arguments is that, today, the defendant, potential defendant, faces a binary choice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In that sense, it lowers the possible downsides for the defendant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It gives another option for the AG to try and move it without having to charge a person.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He may still choose to charge if he thinks it is egregious.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To turn it on its head and to suggest that it is somehow a major change in the law and it is infringement of people's rights and reverses the burden of proof – all simply not true.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A number of speakers, particularly Assoc Prof Daniel Goh and Mr Dennis Tan and a few others, spoke about Benjamin Lim.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, I am afraid I will have to repeat this ad nauseam.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, whatever we discussed under the rubric of, within the framework of sub judice, the same law applies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whatever we could say then, we can say tomorrow.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whatever we could not say then, we cannot say tomorrow.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This huge concern that after tomorrow we cannot have these sorts of discussions and somehow things are going to change, I give you the benefit of doubt and assume that you really felt that, but if so, you can be rest assured that that is not the law and that is not what the Bill seeks to do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Specific to Benjamin Lim, if Members went back to read what I said, I had said that it was not ideal to have an extensive discussion in Parliament on the facts at the time when the Coroner's inquiry had not taken place, for obvious reasons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Witnesses were going to come and Ministerial Statements were made, people were talking about it, there was a large amount of publicity and the Minister setting out this is what happened.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I did not think it was appropriate, but we had to do it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I did not think it was appropriate to discuss facts in detail when there was a Coroner's inquiry pending.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that does not preclude us from discussing whether the Police should themselves interview young people or whether they should have an appropriate adult present.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not preclude us from discussing how schools should handle young people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not prevent us from discussing a wide variety of issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think what is not appropriate is to discuss facts specific to what happened.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin asked about the Government exception on statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think I have made a number of points, it happens regularly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Up to now, no one has thought that there was anything wrong with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In a democratic society, in a day-to-day situation, the Government has a duty to come out and say it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Indeed, this is an appropriate time to read out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A number of people cited, including Ms Sylvia Lim, the case of Lau Swee Soong and tried suggesting that it shows, in fact, the Government does not have the right to make statements that it believes to be in the public interests.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is, if I may say so, not an accurate reading of the Lau Swee Soong case and let me quote, because rather than me saying it, let me quote and you hear it yourself what the law is.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I also think he is right, so we all agree. "To suggest that the Government should not give information to the public by radio and television on matters of great public interest relating to the maintenance of law and order is simply to demand the abandonment by the Government of their duty and the surrender of their authority." I have extended it, almost every instance I have given you, as happened sometime in the past, even though I have put it as hypothetical examples.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People die on MRT tracks or something happens in a hospital.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You just multiply the instances, just think back, each time the Government comes out and says something.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we take advice from AGC and we are quite careful.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin also asked about fair criticism on public affairs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I explained in my speech, the moment you say you allow the public discussion on a pending case, as long as it is in public interest – you see, there is a broad range of public opinion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Effectively, what you are saying is it is okay for the trial to be prejudiced.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because if you are not prejudicing the trial, there is nothing to prevent you from discussing it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we are actually talking about a very narrow area.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Going back to Mr Kok Heng Leun's example, if you gather people round somewhere in a meeting and you sit and discuss an ongoing case, I ask you how is that going to prejudice a fair trial?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if you organise a campaign to get the judge to rule in a certain way, you can see that is wrong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think the Member is suggesting that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What he is suggesting is people come together and there is a topic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Inevitably, they will start talking about Yang Yin or the City Harvest case, yes, whether they do it in a coffee shop or whether they do it by the seaside, I do not think anyone will suggest that is contempt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The law tomorrow is the same as the law through those years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Kuik talked about the young people who feel it is restricting free speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the Member is fair enough to put it as, "It is an emotional reaction".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What I am giving you are cold facts, the law tomorrow is the same as the law yesterday.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, they can discuss a great deal and, as reasonable people, they will agree they should not do anything that prejudices the right of somebody else to have a fair trial.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think if you put it in those terms they will understand.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will have to rely on you and others to put out that point as to what this law entails.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For a start, maybe you can tell them it does not really affect what they do or what they have been doing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Unless they want to start thinking in terms of going public and attacking witnesses and attacking Judges and trying to get certain results from the Court, I do not think the kind of discussions you are talking about, by and large, relate to that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, that does not mean that after the judgment is over, they cannot go and try and organise themselves to say the Government should change the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As to who will check the Government, I think I have given Members the answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I suppose the law of contempt confuses a lot of people, and that is one of the reasons we are trying to put it out in writing clearly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second point Mr Singh made is whether there has been any evidence that witnesses and others have been influenced, why is this law necessary, and were people influenced and, if they were not influenced, then why is it necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Mr Singh has lost the thread of my points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Singh is right if we are doing something through this Bill which is not currently the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why you have a certain sanctity to your proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I am putting it out in writing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If anyone has any objection to me putting out in writing what is the current law, then tell me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have not heard a single argument so far, I have not heard a single argument as to why we should not crystallise the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Singh also said we are bringing in all these legislation, one by one, and we are restricting civil liberties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For Protection from Harassment Act, or POHA, it was presented as something for the people, as helping people who are being harassed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I thought that was what I heard.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think if that is what Mr Singh said, then he should check his facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because my recollection is that the Government has not sued for harassment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And so, the entire facade of arguments that was set up on the basis that POHA – the Government sues for harassment after passing it by stealth and now this – it breaks fundamentally, because, first of all, here the law does not change, except in the one way which I suggested.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I am not sure what the point is.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My own recollection is that the Ministry of Defence asked for a factual clarification under a different provision, not for harassment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh has made many speeches about the importance of transparency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think in that spirit, he will understand that if somebody publishes something about the Government or any Ministry, and if the Ministry wants to respond and ask the person, "Put up my response.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not asking you to change your article but carry my response", as a champion of transparency and open ideas and free exchange of ideas, surely, he would support it, unless he thinks that everyone should have the right, other than the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Singh made the point as well about the Alan Shadrake case and penalties, and the curtailing of civil liberties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think I have explained the Alan Shadrake point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you get away from this obsession with one aspect of contempt and look at it across the spectrum, you will see that maximum penalties have to be set, unless you do not trust the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I say, have confidence in the Courts to impose the appropriate sentence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Asst Prof Mahdev asked me for the bright line between what is permissible and what is not permissible in clauses 3 and 13.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am going to tell the Member that we should stick with how the cases have defined it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the Bill, scandalising, if you impugn the integrity of the Court, say they are biased, you make those sorts of allegations, it is fairly clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sub judice – there are cases, and I have told you and confirmed many times, it is conjunctive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You got to show that conduct, the publication and the real risk of interfering or real risk of prejudice. "Real risk" versus "risk", I think I have explained a number of times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They do not take the larger policy perspectives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are not in a position to take the larger policy perspectives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Executive is uniquely placed to take a broader policy perspective including how we develop, how we should protect.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In that context, I have explained why I have decided it should be "risk".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think you can get any clearer statement than that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think you asked me whether the public can say anything as long as it is not intended, not calculated by them to prejudge proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not so much what they think; it is what the impact is.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Supposing it seriously prejudices the proceedings and the guy comes and says, "Actually, I did not intend that".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think the Courts have accepted that approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I can go along with you in saying that you can say what you like.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, you can say about the universe, a whole variety of things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When it comes to a specific case in Court, you need to be careful.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you sit in a coffee shop and talk, that is not an issue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you look at who is saying it, you look at the reach, you look at the possibility of influencing the Court, you look at the whole host of factors and these are best left to the Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in the broad types of cases that Mr Kok Heng Leun has mentioned, just ask yourself what is the real risk of prejudicing the proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And remember the other point – the law is the same before and tomorrow.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Mr Miyagi, Mr Brown, whatever they have said, have they been charged?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also raised this point of a police state.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All these phrases – "democracy", "freedom of speech", "police state".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What part of this Bill makes it a police state?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you go to a layperson who has not followed the debate and you tell him, "You know, the Government is passing a law which is allowing the Police to come in and do all sorts of things to you", it makes good copy, but it is not the truth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is an offence, somebody has got to investigate and the Police are the parties who will investigate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also brought it down to the personal level as to whether I am passing this law to protect myself because of statements that I had made in the recent past.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think people who know me know that I am quite careful about what I say.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When I say something is unlawful, I mean it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When I go on TV and I talk about the Thaipusam case, I know exactly what I am saying.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The law then and the law tomorrow are the same.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I have been guilty of contempt then, this law is not going to help me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I am not guilty of contempt, this law is completely irrelevant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Ms Lim believes that I have committed contempt, she does not have to wait for the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People went out to attack the Police and made all sorts of allegations while a trial was pending.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As the Minister responsible, or one of the Ministers responsible, it was appropriate that when the Police's integrity is being attacked, I go out in response to those allegations to set out some of the facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As regards the comment, again quite unnecessary, about the Law Society President, I said then that it was not quite appropriate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I felt that the debate was also best avoided.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The law is the same then, the law is the same tomorrow.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, this phrase, "This law is to protect the ruling elite", I suppose that means the front bench, the ruling elite.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I fail to understand because it has got nothing to do with us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has all got to do with the judges and how Court proceedings are conducted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What you say has got to have some reference to the matter at hand.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Scandalising the Court, you go and say something about the Court, you say the judge is biased, what has that got to do with anyone sitting here?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You go and interfere with existing Court proceedings, what has that got to do with us?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I could have well left this law alone except that if I am doing my duty and doing what is right, I would say we need to protect our Judiciary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you go and shout in Court and interrupt Court proceedings, what has that got to do with us?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I tell you who will be afraid of this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are at least two types of people who will be afraid of this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One would be people who pose to be responsible in public but privately encourage others to say things about the Courts and generally in the belief that as long as you bring down institutions, they benefit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are people like that whose public presentation is very different from what they do privately.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a second category who are less smart, who turn up in Court and try and interrupt Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh also talked about chilling effect and so on, but I think I have dealt with most of the points and have explained that if you did not feel any chilling effect the day before, you should not feel any chilling effect the day after because the law is the same.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is just that it is written out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It may be that in the past, not being a lawyer, you had not, thankfully, have had to deal with the law of contempt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And now, seeing it in writing for the first time in your life, perhaps, you say, "Oh, is this what the law provides?" That is the law and that is the reason why it should be in writing because imagine how many people would have understood this law if it was not in writing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, you made the point, members of the public talked about Benjamin Lim, you are a concerned father, what about concerned fathers speaking about the matter?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Well, the rubric of the law, the framework of the law was set and that same framework applies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sometimes, they may be in contempt but the likelihood is the AG takes a look at it, as he often does, and then decides not to do anything about it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You sort of assess and you just go for the more egregious types of cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if a father who has lost his son or daughter, he is grieving and saying all these things happened and he comes out and says all these things, I think the likelihood that that would amount to a serious or a real risk of interfering with any subsequent proceedings, most people can look at it and discount that for the purpose of the proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even if somebody were to take a view that that interferes with the Court proceedings, often in the context of the discussions, it is not likely that any AG will think contempt is warranted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the real point is how has it operated all these years?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Since we have not had a problem, we should not have a problem now and hereafter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Lily Neo asked how the Court will deal with spouses who disobey Court orders because they are unable to pay or due to other reasons which are beyond their control.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are many reasons why people disobey maintenance orders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if they really have no money, then you got to ask whether contempt proceedings are the best.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are spouses out there to whom we want to send a strong message through this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Where the spouse is impecunious or there are extenuating circumstances, the Court will obviously give proper weight to those issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it does not have to impose a fine in every single case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even after a person has been found guilty of contempt, the Court can suspend the sentence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court will give the contemnor time to comply with the order of Court and to comply with such conditions as it thinks fit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Bill also gives the Court discretion to fully discharge a contemnor on the condition that he or she satisfies another order made by the Court, such as a varied order to pay the maintenance in more manageable instalments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Neo also suggested that other forms of punishments or remedial actions for contempt should be included to deal with such spouses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Similarly, Ms Rahayu Mahzam has asked whether my Ministry has further plans to make enforcement of Court orders more effective.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To better deal with the situation described by Dr Neo, other existing ways to enforce maintenance orders under the Women's Charter, such as an attachment order, could also be used.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng asked, "What is fair criticism?" The test is set out in case law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It covers, for example, articles written by academics who criticise judgments and, of course, criticisms by non-academics as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts have set out what is fair criticism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun set out two examples and asked if these would be contempt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Simply stating a hope that justice is to be done, how can that be contempt?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think if you take away one thing from the debate, just ask yourself how has the law operated up to now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is how it is going to operate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is already a lot of public discussion on cases, on proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The test is: does that prejudice or does that pose a real risk of prejudicing?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An obvious example is when you organise to try and pressure the judge or pressure a witness.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think that those are the kinds of cases the Member was talking about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Kok has also asked what about merely disagreeing with how a case has been handled, I think the way you have characterised it, that should not be a problem.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if you believe that the judge should not listen to a certain expert witness, that is also disagreeing with how a case should be handled and if you try to pressure the judge into disbelieving a particular witness, I think that crosses the line.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Kok said that it is not clear what is the compelling reason for this sub judice rule in the light of the eminently qualified Judiciary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The first point is that this is the current law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The reason why we have the system that we have is because we have kept this law and we have enforced it; and Singaporeans have accepted it and we are not changing it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Kok also comes close to saying, "Look, it is okay if there is prejudice", in response to my point that witnesses could be influenced by an organised campaign.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Kok made this point: witnesses are just one aspect of the testimony and it really does not matter if there is prejudice because the witness changes his mind and does not tell the truth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the witnesses are coerced or otherwise persuaded to change their testimony, that is serious prejudice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think we can lightly disregard it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Imagine your friend is the person who is charged and let us say there are five witnesses and they change their testimony or some of them change their testimony.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Would you be satisfied in saying it does not matter, that is only one aspect, there are other aspects, documents and so on?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Your friend must have the right for fair trial, the presumption of innocence, and witnesses, all the witnesses, must come and tell the truth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is no law that can force them to tell the truth but at least we can make sure that we do not have extraneous influences influencing them and changing the way they give evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is really a question of whether the public discussions impose a real risk of prejudicing the proceedings or, in fact, actually prejudicing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One of the speakers asked if the word "publication" is too wide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, it is just crystallising the current law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Publication to a single person will usually not result in any prejudice to proceedings, it is common sense.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But publication to a key witness in an ongoing case to try and persuade that person, you can see that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why we do not try to set it out in detail here, we leave it to the Court, the test being "was the trial prejudiced, or is there a real risk?" If you are the key witness and somebody changes your mind, he is interfering with the proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Darryl David asked whether media outlets, social media companies, other intermediaries will be liable under the Bill for contemptuous material published by their readers or users of their online platforms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Innocent online intermediaries should not be liable for contempt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I can assure the Member that Singapore remains an open operating environment for these online intermediaries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Member also asked if public discussion or advocacy on matters of public interest will be unnecessarily stifled and if such advocacy would amount to interference with or prejudice ongoing proceedings; and Ms Thanaletchimi asked if the public and netizens are only permitted to comment on a case after the case is concluded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just proceed on that basis, that is the law and that is what the Bill provides.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can comment on general policies, you can debate public issues, you can even debate the proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it depends on how many people, what sort of platform, who are the people involved, how likely it is to prejudice the proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun, like others, made this point that discussions in the Benjamin Lim case were useful and Police started reviewing their procedures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will make a factual correction – if you go back and you look at our statements, we decided on that early, it was not because of the public discussion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I agree that there is value to public discussion but the context is when, at what stage, and what sort of discussion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some sorts of discussions are possible before the proceedings are concluded, some sorts of discussion should be held after the proceedings are concluded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even if the kind of discussions relating to going to the issues as it is discussed before the proceedings are concluded, it does not automatically become contempt unless it is of such a scale and nature to prejudice the proceedings, or a real risk of doing so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun also asked whether his project Both Sides Now, which discussed end-of-life issues would have been in breach of sub judice law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not know enough but based on your description, probably not.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And again, nobody cited you for contempt and nobody will cite you for contempt hereafter, I assume people knew about what you did.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Thanaletchimi asked if there are channels for making genuine complaints regarding the conduct of a judge who is hearing an ongoing case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan, Ms Denise Phua, Dr Tan Wu Meng, Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin, Mr Louis Ng and others have asked what is necessary in the public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I took it earlier on and explained it just now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said the Courts are the ultimate arbiters in the sense that any time the Government exercises a power given under a statute, the Courts are the ultimate arbiters.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have to see whether the framework for exercise of the power has been conformed with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I can assure Ms Kuik this clause does not extend to anyone beyond the Executive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is certainly not the Courts or others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Darryl David asked how this Bill will affect the current reporting practices of the mainstream media and the alternative media.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The mainstream media in Singapore has generally been responsible, adhered to high standards in terms of what they report of ongoing proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The practices which were acceptable up to today will continue to be acceptable tomorrow.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Thanaletchimi asked how the terms like "fair and accurate", "good faith", "honest" and "reasonable" and so on under the various clauses in the Bill would be interpreted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of those terms are already interpreted by the Courts and they are best placed to do it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think most people reading it will know what they mean.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I explained earlier, this is an additional route, in addition to the current routes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we left it in the current situation, the AG has only one choice ‒ to charge you for a criminal offence straightaway.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng suggested having penalties for each form of contempt for better clarity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We just set out the maximum penalties and then leave it to the Courts to be sensible and apply different penalties for different types of contempt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It all depends on what happened and the particular facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked whether orders made by the Industrial Arbitration Courts and various other Tribunals would be subject to the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Thanaletchimi raised the same query on Industrial Arbitration Courts orders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What we are really asking is why is there a need for the award to be disobeyed at least two times before it can be punished as contempt of Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I can understand but it, unfortunately, primarily relates to a policy of the Industrial Arbitration Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But my Ministry will be happy to work with the Ministry of Manpower and Mr Patrick Tay to see how we can ensure effective enforcement of the Industrial Arbitration Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Maybe Mr Tay can also discuss with them to see whether the policy can be changed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As for the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunal (CDRT), it is a State Court, so disobedience of CDRT orders will fall under the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think there have been some suggestions on public education, frequently asked questions, and we will release some illustrations of what is and what is not contempt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think I have covered the questions raised by all the Members.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I am not convinced by the Minister's explanation.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I stand by what I say, based on my understanding of the effect and implication of the Bill if passed.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: For instance, there is a definition of publication.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: And according to clause 2 of the Bill, a person is said to have published something when he communicates even orally, or even if it is just one member of the public.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: So, that I think applies to people who talk, discuss at coffee shops.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: And this, I smell a similar element in the Internal Security Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us start with the first point, which I think is quite conclusive, because what Mr Low says is that he is not convinced by me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the face of it, it looks like he is disagreeing, but then that leaves only two interpretations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Either I am right about what the Bill says or I am wrong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if I am right, then none of his arguments can stand.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Therefore, I think that is the most conclusive point in the debate so far: I am right.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I am right because – Mr Low, you are not a lawyer – you look at the three heads of contempt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In clause 3, they set out the current law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am unable to take it further because you disagree without telling me why they are different, whereas I have taken some trouble to explain to you why they are the same.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As for the fourth head of contempt, I have said it is a change and I have explained the change.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have explained how it affects very few people and I have not heard anything else from you.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I think, in a way, that it is conclusive, because, if I am right, the Bill makes no change, then you cannot have any objection.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But you can have an objection if you believe that I am wrong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this is a strange case where a Member of Parliament says the Minister for Law who puts up the Bill, after extensive consultation with the Courts and who says ad nauseam that the law is the same and is intended to be the same, and the argument is, "I do not believe you, I do not trust you, I think you are trying to make a change." How do I argue that point?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, you made that point by reference to specific points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One is publication; it applies to publication to one person and, therefore, coffee shop.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, Mr Low, you cannot just look at one clause on publication.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, how does a person sitting in a coffee shop in Hougang saying that something is wrong in the Courts, how does that statement impact on either the judge or the witnesses or the proceedings?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have given you one example where it can impact.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You catch hold of a witness, you bring him to the coffee shop and you threaten him, yes, it is publication and it is interference of the proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You then said, referring to the powers of the AG, that the Court "must".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But you have not read the rest of it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The AG has got to prove a number of things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And who do you think decides on whether the AG has shown or has not shown those things?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The AG has got to go there to the Courts and show this, this, this, all these conditions have been satisfied, prima facie, and then the Court has got to decide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If it decides that it does not agree with the AG, it throws him out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if it decides that it agrees with the AG, then it says, "Okay, I give you the order".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, the other side is entitled to come back to Court and say, "You know, you have not heard everything.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have a side of the story and this is my story." And if the Court agrees with the respondent, what do you think happens?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Constitution provides that judicial power is vested in our Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Finding of facts, as provided for in this Bill, requires the Court to make those findings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The AG cannot go and say, "Look, give me the order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not need to satisfy you of anything." If he can say that, you are right.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that is not what the clause says.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have said the Bill gives the Government the power to be the sole interpreter of public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I spent a fair bit of time explaining to the Nominated Members how that clause is to be interpreted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I said this was discussed with the Supreme Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, one has got to go back and look at the rubric and decide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, you have made the suggestion of the Internal Security Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I was wondering when that would come up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I can tell you I have not seen any powers of detention without trial in this Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: First of all, on clause 3(4) itself, I do think the Minister is wrong in that my reading of the clause is that it actually increases the power of the Government vis-a-vis public interest, and if I may clarify why I say so.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Next, on a related point, Madam, on the Lau Swee Soong case, I do not think it is anywhere stated in the judgment that bad faith is the only reason for the Court to intervene to curtail Ministers from speaking too much and to be in contempt.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: We quoted from the judgment of Justice Choor Singh.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: It is true that Justice Choor Singh mentioned that if a Minister's statement is calculated to prejudice a fair trial, then he would not escape being punished for contempt.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And as far as I understand the word "calculated", it does not need the Minister to intend the outcome.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But so long as the statement is likely in the circumstances to prejudice a fair trial, then it already will become a potential contentious statement.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, we have a conflict here between, on the one hand, the new clause which says that the Government's belief is what counts and, on the other hand, Lau Swee Soong does not really say that bad faith is the only way in which the Court can supervise the Minister's assessment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Next, the Minister, on a connected note, keeps saying that, the Lau Swee Soong case made reference to the fact that —

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Ms Lim, can you keep your clarifications short?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The Minister was earlier saying that in the Lau Swee Soong judgment, the Court recognised that the Government has a duty to act in the public interest, otherwise people might die and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But at the same time, does he not agree that in the judgment itself, the Court also expressly said that Dr Goh Keng Swee's statements in those cases were still within the Government's duty because they were referring to the general circumstances of the riot and did not touch on the individuals' actions in the riot.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, Mr Lau did not have a cause to complain because there was no statement made about what Mr Lau did or did not do.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: This is in sharp contrast with some of the statements that the Minister himself has made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Clause 3(4) read with Justice Choor Singh's judgment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at clause 3(4), what does it say?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government has got to show that it believes that such a statement is necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if challenged, the Government would have to show that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Justice Choor Singh said if a statement is calculated to prejudice the proceedings, then the Minister would be liable for contempt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If a statement is calculated to affect, prejudice proceedings, how can the Government show that it believes that the statement is necessary in the public interest if it is calculated to interfere and prejudice proceedings?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Well, Ms Lim, that is my view and I have stated it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think the law is that all that the Government has got to show is that it believes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You look at all the cases in the past as to what the Government has got to show.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts will give considerable deference to what the Government states but, ultimately, they decide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Next, in terms of the Thaipusam case, I do not know what the relevance is, because if Ms Sylvia Lim believes that what I have said was contempt, please file the case with the AG.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us not debate the merits of what I said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I believe what I said was not contempt and I do not believe that what I said caused prejudice or a real risk of prejudice to anyone's trial.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you believe otherwise, file it but certainly do not link this Bill with that because the genesis of this Bill was six years ago, well before the Thaipusam case, and 2012 and 2013.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A number of situations have been investigated by the Police on the directions of AG.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The general provisions allow the Police because it is a criminal offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not specified in CPC as an arrestable offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Any offence can only be investigated by the Police.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police went in and took all the documents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that was, if I am not wrong, 1995.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I handled contempt cases for nearly 25 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When there is contempt, the AG gets involved, he asks the Police.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, here, now, we are setting it out in writing and as we set it out in writing, we have made it an arrestable offence, like other arrestable offences but —

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Well, if you want to make that point, please go ahead and make it, but those are the facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Police are the people who always investigate offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can argue as to whether it should be arrestable or non-arrestable.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin
text: Can I confirm that a publication made as part of a discussion in good faith on a matter of general public affairs is not contempt of Court under clause 3(1)(b) if there is no prejudice or interference or real risk of prejudice or interference?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: You said something about the "planned, orchestrated campaign" by The Online Citizen in the midst of all the different falsehoods that were being perpetuated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Would you say that with this law now, with clause 13, you could ask the AG to start proceedings − non-publication vis-a-vis The Online Citizen?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Would you say that The Online Citizen was in contempt at that point of time sub judice?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: And if they were, why were not proceedings being launched against them and will this law be used against them if it was law then?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That question has to be answered by reference to the law in place in March which is going to be the same law in place tomorrow.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whether they are in contempt, I should not be giving legal advice from the table.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But what I can say, as a matter of policy, is that the law has not changed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If what they did was contempt, that is for the AG to consider.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you have put in a question on that, if public policy considerations allow an answer – because sometimes we should not be answering if the AG is considering the matter – but subject to that, I will be happy to answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This law does not change the position nor will it apply to what has happened in the past.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And, finally, what prevented the Ministry from publishing the feedback it collected over the last six years under the Bill and sharing it with the public as it has on its website in the case of other legislation?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can I know what the second question was, please?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second question was: does the Minister not agree that its public consultation process leaves a lot of room to be desired in view of the negative feedback the Bill has generated thus far?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Look, I cannot remember but I assume it was circulated publicly probably after the First Reading but I cannot be sure.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do I agree that there is much room for public consultation given the negative feedback that it has generated?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think I do not agree with all the different parts of that question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First of all, I think, and as a lawyer, you would know sometimes it is better to ask a single question, not three questions together.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the negative feedback, we have done surveys.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to make a judgement call on what "public interest" is.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are essentially crystallising the existing law except for the one change in the substantive law on contempt and some of the changes in process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not believe if you tell the truth and you explain it as it is, I do not think there will be negative reaction.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if you go and tell people, "you know, your rights are going to be curbed, that democracy is under attack, do you know that the law substantially curbs your freedom", if you say all those things and they do not read the Bill, of course, then they will get concerned.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I agree in so far as there is any suggestion in your question that we have to go out and persuade people on what the Bill really involves, which we will try.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why not circulate the feedback collected over six years?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I was not suggesting that we have been collecting feedback over six years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have been talking to people but it was really in the back burner in terms of leaving it to AGC to draft and I explained why it was not something that we pushed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Other legislation − changes in Criminal Procedure Code, changes in the Penal Code, they were all important because they make a change to the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This one is essentially a codification of the law, subject to those changes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, therefore, it was not essential or necessary for us to rush with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We took our time and when we drafted it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We took the views of the people that I had listed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not suggest that is comprehensive and some of the feedback is − people when they give us the feedback, they expect us to keep it to ourselves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of the feedback, I think we could consider putting it up but, essentially, we took the approach, we took the view that the Bill − if you look at three of the four heads – it is the same.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at most of the other things, it is the same.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This is with regard to the provision for the AG's right to apply for non-publication order.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I think given that we are going to codify this into a criminal statute, personally, I am of the view that it is inappropriate to compare this with a civil injunction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: My question remains as per my speech just now which is: why does the Government wish to bar the defendant from attending the hearing of the AG's application?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The AG may have to move very quickly to go to Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A recalcitrant defendant, first of all, can play games in terms of avoiding service, avoiding coming to Court and try and delay the matter for weeks sometimes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you need to be practical about it and balance both sides' interests.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is the best way of balancing the interests?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the one side, irreparable damage being caused by the publication being on and being circulated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the other side, the defendant's right to be heard.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, you balance it by giving the defendant the right after he receives the order and takes it down, or he can choose, if he says, "I am going to challenge it, I am not in contempt", then he comes to Court and he challenges.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If he succeeds, he puts it back up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have got to look at it like that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whereas, if you do not allow the quick remedy, interim relief, that article could be there for weeks by which point in time, there is no point taking it down anyway.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I will just need to do a double confirming.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: If there is a dispute as to whether what the Government believes on an issue is necessary in the public interest, then the judge can take a view and the judge can also refer to the common law, especially Judge Choor Singh's case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Kok, I will answer your question in this way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Look at clause 3(4), a statement made by a person on behalf of the Government and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the Government believes that such a statement is necessary in the public interest, so you got to show that the Government believes that it is necessary in the public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have got to show what the public interest is, and that it is necessary, and that the Government believed it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am just using that passage in Justice Choor Singh's case as an aid – if it is apparent that the statements were really calculated to prejudice the ongoing proceedings but the Government is coming to Court and saying that, "I am actually saying it because it is in the public interest and I believe it to be so", then, the Court can make a finding that the Government did not really believe.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is case law on how the Courts arrive at such findings and one has got to go back to those things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ultimately, the Government's exercise of this power and most powers derive from statutes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts will have to look carefully at the clause and see whether the Government comes within, or outside.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: One is actually a clarification about the clarification the Minister gave to Ms Sylvia Lim regarding section 3(4).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, if I understand the Minister correctly, what the Minister said is that the Courts will ultimately decide, which means to say that the Courts will decide whether something the Government has done because it thinks it is in the national interest is really in the national interest.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If that is the case, if the Minister is of the view that the Court should ultimately decide why was the language chosen, why was it worded such that it says that what the Government thinks is in the national interest rather than what objectively is in the national interest.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I believe this also goes to the amendment made by the Nominated Members.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My last explanation to Nominated Member Kok Heng Leun stands.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My second point of clarification is with regard to the penalties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it was a point made by former Chief Justice Chan Sek Keong.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a point made in various jurisdictions that the law should limit and set out the maximum penalties as opposed to leaving it unlimited.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, it is not correct to say, and I have made the point a number of times, that the penalties provided are at variance with the penalties that the Courts have imposed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You are looking at one type of case, but there are many other types of contempt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I were to ask any reasonable person here, going back to my example just now, $100 million and there is an injunction and the defendant takes out $50 million in breach of the injunction and he is brought to Court, what do you think the penalty ought to be?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Supposing a penalty is imposed, he goes away and then he takes away another $25 million.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What do you think the penalty ought to be?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, do you think eight months was excessive for the recalcitrant in the Family Courts?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How is this penalty, the maximum penalty that is prescribed here, at substantial variance with that eight months?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is not accurate to say it is at variance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As for this chilling effect, well, it will have a chilling effect on those who would constitutionally want to stand up every day and say that the judge is biased.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it would have had that same chilling effect yesterday as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As for the rest who want to discuss matters of public interest in good faith, I do not see why there should be any chilling effect.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, the law is set out in writing, whereas, yesterday, it was not.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: The Minister earlier said that the Bill has the support of the majority of the population.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am glad that the Member asked that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We did a scientifically valid statistical survey and a very substantial majority – the thing is, I do not have the survey with me right now – supported it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I do not want to quote the figures because I cannot remember the figures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it was a survey conducted by us and the results of the survey were that we had substantial support.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Ms Lim, are you making the same clarification because —

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Please keep it short because we are going round in circles

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The only thing I want to ask the Minister is he said that there was a survey done and the majority of the people support it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Can he confirm whether the draft Bill was actually shown to these people and were they just asked some general questions about protecting the integrity of our Courts?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My understanding – and I do not want to misstate it – my understanding is that the questions related to putting in statutory form the law of contempt and if you look at it, we are now setting it out in writing.
